book.subtitle: From multivariable change to conservation in space
book.author: AI University · AI-generated
book.description: A complete course in multivariable and vector calculus: spatial geometry, vector curves, partial derivatives and optimization, multiple integrals, line and surface integrals, Green's, Stokes' and divergence theorems, and conservation.
book.audience: Learners familiar with single-variable differentiation, integration, substitution and parametric curves
book.scope: Nine complete chapters covering spatial motion, Jacobians, flux and integral theorems. Full linear algebra, torsion theory, differential forms, second-order equations and PDE solution methods belong to separate volumes.

chapters.title: Vectors and space
chapters.subtitle: Coordinates for directions, projections and surfaces
chapters.intro: Separate position, direction and shape. Dot products measure alignment; cross products give normals. Lines, planes and coordinate systems prepare for spatial calculus.
goals: Write equations of lines and planes

chapters.title: Spatial curves and motion
chapters.subtitle: Position, velocity and bending
chapters.intro: Differentiate components, then interpret geometrically. Velocity is tangent; acceleration changes speed or direction.

chapters.title: Multivariable change and differentiation
chapters.subtitle: From coordinate slices to a common linear approximation
chapters.intro: Partials inspect coordinate directions. Differentiability requires one linear model for every small displacement. Gradients and the chain rule put that model to work.

chapters.title: Local models and optimization
chapters.subtitle: Find candidates, then inspect directions and boundaries
chapters.intro: Second-order terms describe bending. Global extrema also require boundary checks. Constraints restrict feasible directions to curves or surfaces.

chapters.title: Double integrals
chapters.subtitle: Accumulate contributions over a planar region
chapters.intro: Multiply each small area by height or density and sum. Drawing the region guides order and coordinate choices.
goals: Use polar coordinates and density models

chapters.title: Triple integrals and substitution
chapters.subtitle: Divide space into small volumes
chapters.intro: Project to find the base, then bound height. Cylindrical, spherical and general substitutions must account for actual volume scaling.

chapters.title: Vector fields and line integrals
chapters.subtitle: Two ways to accumulate along a path
chapters.intro: Scalar integrals weight by length; work dots force with displacement. Potentials and Green's theorem replace paths by endpoint or region calculations.

chapters.title: Surfaces and flux
chapters.subtitle: Area needs scaling; flux needs orientation too
chapters.intro: Two parameters generate a surface. Tangent cross products supply area scaling and normals, reducing surface integrals to double integrals.
goals: Compute surface area and scalar integrals
Compute oriented flux, divergence and curl

chapters.title: From local change to boundaries
chapters.subtitle: Green's, Stokes' and divergence theorems
chapters.intro: Shared internal edges or faces cancel, connecting local change with total boundary behavior. Check smoothness, closure and orientation before choosing a calculation.

questions.hint: Speed is constant.

questions.problem: A radius-2 circle is traveled at speed 3. Find normal acceleration magnitude.
questions.hint: Compute curvature first.

questions.hint: Find velocity and acceleration, then use perpendicularity.

reviews.title: Multivariable change and differentiation: chapter review

questions.problem: Find the derivative of $f=x^2+xy+3y^2$ at $(1,-1)$ along $(1,1)$.
questions.hint: Normalize the direction first.
solution: Gradient $(1,-5)$ dotted with $(1,1)/\sqrt2$.
This gives $-4/\sqrt2=-2\sqrt2$.

questions.problem: Find the tangent plane of $z=e^{xy}$ at $(0,1)$.
questions.hint: Evaluate value and both partials at the center.
solution: Value one; first partial one; second partial zero.
Tangent plane $z=1+x$.

questions.problem: For $f=\frac{x^2y^2}{x^2+y^2}$, extended by zero at the origin, is it differentiable?
questions.hint: Bound the remainder uniformly by distance.
solution: Both axis partials are zero, and $x^2y^2\le(x^2+y^2)^2/4$.
Magnitude is at most one-quarter distance squared; division by distance tends to zero.

reviews.title: Local models and optimization: chapter review

questions.problem: Find the global minimum of $f=x^2+4y^2-2x+8y$.
questions.hint: Complete squares rather than just solving for stationary points.
solution: The squared terms are nonnegative, with equality at $(1,-1)$.

questions.problem: Find maximum and minimum of $f=xy$ on $x^2+y^2\le2$.
questions.hint: Bound the product above and below, then find equality points.
solution: $(x-y)^2\ge0$ gives $xy\le1$; $(x+y)^2\ge0$ gives $xy\ge-1$.
The bounds are attained at $(1,1)$ and $(1,-1)$ respectively.

questions.problem: Find the second-order origin model of $f=e^{x-y}$.
questions.hint: Apply the one-variable exponential expansion to the difference.
solution: The mixed coefficient is minus one.

questions.problem: Integrate $y$ over region $0\le y\le x\le2$.
questions.hint: Integrate the second coordinate, then the first.

questions.problem: Find the center of mass of the unit disk with area density $\sigma=1+x$.
questions.hint: Cancel odd moments and evaluate the squared-coordinate integral.
solution: Mass is $\pi$; the second-coordinate moment is zero.
The first-coordinate moment is the disk integral of $x^2$, equal to $\pi/4$.

questions.problem: Reverse and evaluate $\int_0^1\int_y^1 \cos(x^2)\,dxdy$.
questions.hint: The region has second coordinate below the first.
solution: Rewrite as $\int_0^1\int_0^x\cos(x^2)\,dydx$.
The result is $\int_0^1x\cos(x^2)dx=\sin1/2$.

questions.problem: Find mean squared origin distance inside a radius-2 ball.
questions.hint: Divide the squared-distance integral by volume.
solution: The integral is $4\pi\cdot2^5/5=128\pi/5$.
Divide by volume $32\pi/3$ to obtain $12/5$.

questions.problem: Write spherical bounds for the first-octant unit ball.
questions.hint: Bound azimuth, inclination and radial distance.

questions.problem: Find the area of the image of the unit square under $x=2u+v,y=u+2v$.
questions.hint: Compute the determinant.

questions.problem: Find work of $(y,x,0)$ along any path from $(1,0,0)$ to $(2,3,0)$.
questions.hint: Find a product potential.
solution: Potential $xy$ has endpoint difference $6-0$.

questions.problem: Evaluate $\oint -2y\,dx+2x\,dy$ around a radius-2 counterclockwise circle.
questions.hint: Use Green to compute rotation density.
solution: Rotation density is 4; area is $4\pi$.

questions.problem: Find work of $(-y/(x^2+y^2),x/(x^2+y^2))$ around a radius-2 counterclockwise circle.
questions.hint: Parametrize the circle; radius factors cancel.
solution: The field is $(-\sin t/2,\cos t/2)$; velocity is $(-2\sin t,2\cos t)$.
Their dot product is one; integrate through one turn.
questions.answer: $2\pi$; changing radius does not remove circulation around the hole.

questions.problem: Find the area of $z=3x$ over a square of side 2.
questions.hint: The area factor is constant.
solution: Factor $\sqrt{10}$ times base area 4.

questions.problem: Find upward flux of $(0,0,4)$ through $z=x+y$ over the unit square.
questions.hint: Use the oriented area vector directly.
solution: The cross product is $(-1,-1,1)$; its field dot product is 4.
The base area is one.

questions.problem: Find divergence and curl of $(z,x,y)$.
questions.hint: Apply each definition separately.
solution: All pure partials vanish, giving zero divergence.
All three curl components equal one.

questions.problem: Find positive circulation of $(-y/2,x/2,z)$ around a horizontal radius-2 circle.
questions.hint: The vertical curl component is one.
solution: Disk area is $4\pi$; Stokes gives circulation $4\pi$.

questions.problem: Find inward flux of $(x,2y,3z)$ through the unit sphere.
questions.hint: Compute outward flux, then reverse.
solution: Divergence is 6; outward flux $8\pi$.
Negate for inward flux.

questions.problem: A fixed container receives mass 7, loses 4 and produces 1 per unit time. Find mass derivative.

exam.problem: Find distance from point $(1,2,2)$ to plane $2x-y+2z=1$.
exam.hint: Divide absolute residual by normal length.
solution: Residual is $2-2+4-1=3$.
Normal length 3 gives distance one.

exam.problem: Find triangle area with vertices at the origin, $(1,1,0)$, $(0,1,1)$.
solution: Cross product $(1,-1,1)$ has length $\sqrt3$.

exam.problem: Find distance traveled by $(\cos t,\sin t,2t)$ from zero to $\pi$.
solution: Multiply speed $\sqrt5$ by time $\pi$.

exam.problem: Find the gradient and steepest rate of $f=x^2y+y^2$ at $(2,1)$.
exam.hint: Compute both partials and gradient length.
solution: Gradient $(4,6)$.
Maximum directional derivative $\sqrt{16+36}=2\sqrt{13}$.

exam.problem: For $f=\frac{xy^2}{x^2+y^2}$, extended by zero at the origin, check continuity and differentiability.
exam.hint: Squeeze first, then inspect diagonal linearization error.
solution: Magnitude is at most $|x|$, giving continuity; both partials are zero.
Along $x=y=t$, the function is $t/2$. Its absolute error-to-distance ratio is $1/(2\sqrt2)$, not tending to zero.

exam.hint: Use the second-derivative test or complete squares.
solution: $D=6\cdot6-2^2=32>0$; the first pure second partial is positive.

exam.problem: Find the maximum of $x+2y+2z$ on the unit sphere.
exam.hint: Dot the constant objective gradient with a unit position.
solution: Gradient length 3 gives upper bound 3.
Equality occurs at $(1/3,2/3,2/3)$.

exam.hint: Evaluate the inner integral or use the triangle's centroid.
solution: The inner integral is $x(1-x)+(1-x)^2/2$.
Integrate the first coordinate from zero to one to get $1/3$.

exam.hint: The radial area factor cancels the density denominator.
solution: $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_1^3 1\,drd\theta=4\pi$.

exam.problem: Find mass in the unit ball with volume density $\rho=x^2+y^2+z^2$.
solution: Squared radial density times squared radial volume factor gives radial integral $1/5$.
The angular factor is $4\pi$.

exam.problem: Find work of field $(2xy,x^2,1)$ from $(0,0,0)$ to $(2,1,3)$.
exam.hint: A potential must match all three components.
solution: Potential $x^2y+z$.
Endpoint difference $4+3=7$.

exam.problem: Find work of $(-y,x,0)$ around the unit circle clockwise twice.
exam.hint: Compute one turn, then account for orientation and repetition.
solution: One counterclockwise turn gives $2\pi$; two reversed turns give $-4\pi$.

exam.problem: Find the upward unit normal of $z=2x-y$ over the unit square.
solution: The unnormalized normal is $(-2,1,1)$, with length $\sqrt6$.

exam.problem: Find outward flux of $(x,y,z)$ through the entire boundary of shell $1\le r\le2$.
exam.hint: Multiply divergence by shell volume, or handle inner and outer orientations separately.
solution: Volume is $28\pi/3$; divergence 3.
The inner normal points toward the center, giving total flux $32\pi-4\pi=28\pi$.

exam.problem: Find work of $(0,0,x)$ around the positive unit-circle boundary in plane $z=0$.
exam.hint: The displacement has no vertical component.
solution: The direct dot product is zero everywhere.
Curl $(0,-1,0)$ also dots to zero with the upward disk normal.

exam.problem: For density $\rho=e^{-2t}$ and velocity $(x,y,0)$ in a fixed region, does source-free conservation hold?
exam.hint: Compute time derivative and mass-flux divergence.
solution: The time derivative is $-2e^{-2t}$; divergence is $2e^{-2t}$.
Their sum is zero, satisfying continuity.

glossary.meaning: A vector records direction and distance of motion. The same displacement can start at different positions.
The dot product measures alignment. Projection gives the part pointing along a chosen direction.
The cross product is perpendicular to both input vectors. Its length is their parallelogram's area.
A line moves from one point in a fixed direction. Every displacement within a plane is perpendicular to its normal.
Fix one coordinate to obtain a cross-section. Key slices are more reliable than memorized silhouettes.
Cylindrical coordinates suit axial shapes; spherical coordinates suit shapes naturally described by distance from the origin.
A vector-valued function gives position. Its derivative is instantaneous velocity, pointing along the path.
Velocity is position's rate of change. Speed is its length. Integrating speed gives distance; integrating velocity gives displacement.
Curvature measures tangent-direction change per unit distance. It describes the curve's shape.
A two-variable function assigns height to each allowed planar position. A contour joins positions with the same height.
A multivariable limit controls every approach within the domain. Two conflicting paths disprove it; finitely many agreeing paths do not prove it.
A partial derivative measures instantaneous change in one variable while all others stay fixed.
Differentiability means one linear expression explains the increment, with remainder negligible relative to displacement length.

glossary.term: The multivariable chain rule and implicit functions
glossary.meaning: When a quantity depends on several intermediate variables, sum the products of local rates along every dependency path.
For a differentiable function, the gradient encodes every directional first-order rate in one vector.
Second-order Taylor polynomials record directional curvature and interactions beyond the tangent plane.

glossary.term: Critical points and the second-derivative test
glossary.meaning: A differentiable interior extremum must have zero gradient. Second-order shape distinguishes a bowl bottom, top or saddle.
A continuous function on a nonempty closed bounded region attains its maximum and minimum. Compare all candidates.
On a smooth equality constraint, an extremal objective gradient is normally parallel to the constraint gradient. Multipliers express that alignment.
A double integral accumulates density or signed height over a planar region into one number.

glossary.term: General regions and changing integration order
glossary.meaning: Limits describe a region. Changing integration order requires reading its boundaries afresh.
Polar coordinates simplify circular boundaries, but actual patch area is radius times radial width times angular width.

glossary.term: Density, centers of mass and inertia
glossary.meaning: Density times area gives mass; multiplying by position gives first moment; multiplying by squared axis distance gives moment of inertia.
Triple integrals accumulate spatial density. Integrating one gives volume.
Cylindrical coordinates retain height and use polar coordinates horizontally. The volume element keeps one radial factor.
The spherical volume element contains distance squared and sine of inclination, arising from two different angular arcs.

glossary.term: General changes of variables and Jacobians
glossary.meaning: A Jacobian determinant gives a smooth coordinate map's local area or volume scaling. Integration uses its absolute value.
A vector field assigns a vector to each point. A streamline's tangent follows the field at each point.
A scalar line integral weights a wire's density by arc length. Reversing direction leaves it unchanged.
A work integral dots force with each directed displacement. Reversing the path reverses its sign.
For a field equal to the gradient of a single-valued function, work is final potential minus initial potential.
Green's theorem converts positive boundary circulation to an integral of local rotation. A second form computes outward planar flux.
Two parameters generate a spatial surface. Their independent tangent vectors have a cross product giving the local normal.

glossary.term: Surface area and scalar surface integrals
glossary.meaning: A surface element is the length of the tangent cross product times parameter area. Scalar surface integrals add a weight.
Flux integrates the field's component along a chosen normal. Tangential flow does not cross the surface.
Divergence measures net outflow per unit volume. Curl's normal component measures local circulation per unit area.
Stokes' theorem connects boundary circulation with curl flux through a surface.

glossary.term: The divergence theorem and closed surfaces
glossary.meaning: The divergence theorem equates outward flux through a closed surface with the integral of divergence over its enclosed volume.
Path work, curl flux and closed-surface flux are different objects. Identify dimension, direction and field before choosing a theorem.
The continuity equation connects local density change with divergence of flux. Integrating gives mass balance on a fixed region.
$R(\mathbf h)=o(\|\mathbf h\|^p)$ means the remainder divided by distance to power $p$ tends to zero.
The matrix of all second partials; symmetric under continuous second partial derivatives.
A nondegenerate point: nonzero curve velocity, nonzero parameter-surface cross product, or nonzero level-constraint gradient, as appropriate.
A connected domain in which every loop contracts continuously to a point within the domain. Planar regions with holes generally fail this.
In finite-dimensional Euclidean space, a closed bounded set. Continuous functions attain extrema on nonempty compact sets.
Accumulate a field's chosen unit-normal component over actual area. Reversing the normal reverses its sign.

appendices.title: Determinants, Jacobians and derivative matrices
appendices.text: The determinant of matrix $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ is $ad-bc$. Expanding a three-dimensional determinant by its first row gives $a(ei-fh)-b(di-fg)+c(dh-eg)$. Each matrix-product entry is a row-column dot product; derivative-matrix multiplication sums over intermediate variables in the chain rule. These local tools do not replace a full linear-algebra course.

appendices.title: The scope of mixed-partial, implicit-function and Taylor results
appendices.text: This volume cites interchange of continuous mixed partials, local implicit functions at regular points and multivariable Taylor's theorem. Restriction to segment $g(t)=f(\mathbf a+t\mathbf h)$ reduces Taylor to one variable; the chain rule generates mixed terms. If that parameter function's third derivative is bounded by $M$, its remainder is at most $M/6$. This $M$ already includes the displacement vector; do not multiply by distance cubed again.

appendices.title: Green's proof on rectangles and extension limits
appendices.text: For rectangle $[a,b]\times[c,d]$, horizontal sides contribute $\int_a^b[P(x,c)-P(x,d)]dx=-\iint P_y\,dA$, vertical sides $\int_c^d[Q(b,y)-Q(a,y)]dy=\iint Q_x\,dA$. Adding yields Green's theorem. Shared edges cancel across pieces. General piecewise smooth boundaries additionally need suitable approximation and integrability arguments; a drawn mesh is not a complete general proof.

appendices.title: Why graph-surface Stokes reduces to Green
appendices.text: For graph $\mathbf r(u,v)=(u,v,g(u,v))$, pullback line-integral coefficients are $A=P+Rg_u,B=Q+Rg_v$, with field components evaluated on the surface. For a twice continuously differentiable graph, expanding $B_u-A_v$ and applying the chain rule yields $(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)$, with mixed second partials cancelling. Apply Green on the parameter domain. The general theorem for piecewise regular surfaces also needs compatible coverage and orientation; that form is cited here.

appendices.title: Divergence, singularities and point sources
appendices.text: For a box, pair its six face fluxes with the single-variable fundamental theorem. Across pieces, internal faces cancel. General boundaries require approximation arguments. Field $\mathbf F=\mathbf r/\|\mathbf r\|^3$ has zero divergence away from the origin; on a radius-$R$ sphere its normal component is $1/R^2$ and flux $4\pi$. It is undefined at the origin, so a containing ball fails the classical theorem's hypotheses. A zero-volume singularity cannot simply be deleted from those hypotheses.

appendices.title: What numerical visuals can and cannot establish
appendices.text: Figures use finite meshes and floating-point numbers. Midpoint sums for linear functions may be exact; polygonal sphere areas are usually approximate. A model's analytic formulas supply readouts labeled exact. Animations reach stated control endpoints; parameters approaching zero retain positive lower bounds. No finite operation completes an infinite limit. Three-dimensional projection preserves equal axis scales; top view loses height, recoverable by rotation.

lessons.title: Spatial coordinates and vectors
lessons.subtitle: Points give positions; vectors give displacements
lessons.concept: A vector records direction and distance of motion. The same displacement can start at different positions.
lessons.intuition: Each coordinate measures travel along one perpendicular axis. Adding components joins two displacements end to end.

body.title: Point or vector?
body.text: A point is a position. The vector from $A$ to $B$ is $B-A$; moving both endpoints equally leaves it unchanged.

body.title: Computing length
body.text: Apply Pythagoras in three directions. Length is nonnegative and vanishes only for the zero vector. Distance is the length of the difference between points.

body.title: Why use unit vectors?
body.text: Divide a nonzero vector by its length to retain direction alone. Negative scaling reverses direction; zero has no normalizable direction.

formalDefinition.text: Points give positions; vectors give displacements
conditions: Use orthogonal Cartesian coordinates and Euclidean distance. Normalization requires $\mathbf v\ne\mathbf0$.

derivation.text: Subtract to find displacement.
Join displacements end to end.
Scaling components scales length by the absolute factor.

lessons.title: Dot products and projections
lessons.subtitle: Extract contribution along a direction
lessons.concept: The dot product measures alignment. Projection gives the part pointing along a chosen direction.
lessons.intuition: Aligned motion contributes positively, perpendicular motion zero, and opposing motion negatively. The dot product summarizes this as a scalar.
objectives: Use dot products to test perpendicularity

body.title: Why is the dot product a scalar?
body.text: Multiply corresponding components and add. This equals one length times the other's signed component along it. The result has sign but no vector direction.

body.title: Testing perpendicularity
body.text: Two nonzero vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product is zero. Zero dots to zero with everything, so exclude it when interpreting angles.

body.title: Scalar versus vector projection
body.text: Scalar projection is a signed length. Vector projection multiplies it by a target unit vector. The residual is perpendicular to that target.

formalDefinition.text: Extract contribution along a direction
formalDefinition.latex: \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\sum_{i=1}^{3}u_iv_i=\|\mathbf u\|\|\mathbf v\|\cos\theta,\quad\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}\mathbf v=\frac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}\mathbf u
conditions: Angles and projection directions require $\mathbf u\ne0$; angles also require $\mathbf v\ne0$; $0\le\theta\le\pi$.

derivation.text: Place vectors at one origin and apply the cosine law.
derivation.latex: \|\mathbf u-\mathbf v\|^2=\|\mathbf u\|^2+\|\mathbf v\|^2-2\|\mathbf u\|\|\mathbf v\|\cos\theta

derivation.text: Expand squared components to obtain the dot product.
Require the projection residual perpendicular to the target.

workedExamples.title: Testing perpendicularity

commonMistakes.claim: A dot product is just the product of lengths.
commonMistakes.correction: Include the angle's cosine; opposing directions give a negative result.

commonMistakes.claim: Projection always preserves length.
commonMistakes.correction: Projection length cannot exceed the original length; perpendicular projection is zero.

steps.title: Aligned
steps.observation: The dot product is positive; projection points forward.

steps.title: Perpendicular
steps.observation: The dot product is numerically zero and the projection vanishes.

steps.title: Opposing
