lessons.title: Cross products, area and normals
lessons.subtitle: Find area and perpendicular direction together
lessons.concept: The cross product is perpendicular to both input vectors. Its length is their parallelogram's area.
lessons.intuition: Base times height gives magnitude; the right-hand rule gives direction. Swapping inputs preserves area and reverses the normal.

body.title: How does it differ from the dot product?
body.text: The dot product is a scalar measuring alignment. The three-dimensional cross product is a vector describing perpendicular direction and spanned area.

body.title: Why does order matter?
body.text: Turn from the first vector toward the second; the right hand chooses the positive normal. Reversing order changes sign.

body.title: Using the triple product
body.text: Dot a cross product with a third vector for signed volume. Its absolute value is parallelepiped volume. Zero means the vectors are coplanar.

formalDefinition.text: Find area and perpendicular direction together
formalDefinition.latex: \mathbf u\times\mathbf v=\langle u_2v_3-u_3v_2,u_3v_1-u_1v_3,u_1v_2-u_2v_1\rangle,\quad A=\|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\|,\quad V=|\mathbf w\cdot(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)|
conditions: Use three-dimensional right-handed Cartesian coordinates. A unit normal requires a nonzero cross product.

derivation.text: Choose a direction perpendicular to both vectors.
derivation.latex: (\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)\cdot\mathbf u=(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v)\cdot\mathbf v=0

derivation.text: Base times height determines magnitude.
Take the third vector's signed height.

workedExamples.title: Triangle area
workedExamples.problem: Find the triangle area spanned by $\mathbf u=\langle2,0,0\rangle,\mathbf v=\langle1,3,0\rangle$.
steps: The parallelogram area is 6; take half.

workedExamples.title: Spatial volume
workedExamples.problem: Find the parallelepiped volume for $\mathbf u=\langle1,0,1\rangle,\mathbf v=\langle0,2,0\rangle,\mathbf w=\langle0,0,3\rangle$.
steps: Dotting with the third gives 6; take its absolute value.

commonMistakes.claim: Swapping cross-product inputs changes nothing.
commonMistakes.correction: The cross product is anticommutative; order determines orientation.

commonMistakes.claim: Parallel vectors give a unique unit normal.
commonMistakes.correction: Their cross product is zero; the perpendicular direction is not unique.

practice.problem: Find $\mathbf i\times\mathbf k$.
practice.hint: Use the right-hand order or components.
solution: Swapping the third and first coordinate directions reverses sign.
The result is $-\mathbf j$.

practice.problem: Find the parallelogram area spanned by $\langle3,0,0\rangle$ and $\langle0,4,0\rangle$.
solution: The cross product is $\langle0,0,12\rangle$, with length 12.

practice.problem: Does swapping two vectors in a triple product change volume?
solution: The signed triple product changes sign.
Its absolute value, geometric volume, stays unchanged.

practice.problem: Two nonzero vectors have zero cross product. What follows?
solution: $\sin\theta=0$; the angle is zero or $\pi$.
They are parallel, either aligned or opposing.

learningCheck.question: What does reversing cross-product order do?
learningCheck.explanation: The normal reverses; area stays nonnegative.

interactiveVisual.caption: Rotate the second vector in its plane and inspect the parallelogram and perpendicular cross product.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Do opposite parallel vectors span positive area?

teaching.explain: Magnitude gives base times height; the right hand chooses direction. Keep area separate from orientation.

steps.title: Parallel
steps.observation: The parallelogram collapses; the cross product is zero.

steps.title: Maximum area
steps.observation: Perpendicular inputs span maximum area.

steps.title: Collapsed again
steps.observation: Opposite parallel inputs still give zero area; the cross product cannot be normalized.

lessons.title: Lines and planes in space
lessons.subtitle: Directions define lines; normals define planes
lessons.concept: A line moves from one point in a fixed direction. Every displacement within a plane is perpendicular to its normal.
lessons.intuition: One direction controls a line; one perpendicular direction constrains all motion in a plane.
objectives: Write equations of lines and planes

body.title: Why parametrize a line?
body.text: One parameter controls three coordinates. Zero direction components are allowed; do not force a symmetric form that divides by zero.

body.title: Deriving a plane equation
body.text: The displacement from a known plane point to any other plane point dots to zero with the normal. Cross two nonparallel in-plane directions to find a normal.

body.title: Computing distance
body.text: Project displacement from a plane point onto its unit normal and take absolute value. Test line direction dotted with normal to analyze parallelism and intersections.

formalDefinition.text: Directions define lines; normals define planes
formalDefinition.latex: \mathbf r(t)=\mathbf p+t\mathbf d,\quad\mathbf n\cdot(\mathbf r-\mathbf p)=0,\quad d(Q,\Pi)=\frac{|\mathbf n\cdot(Q-\mathbf p)|}{\|\mathbf n\|}
conditions: Line direction $\mathbf d\ne0$ and plane normal $\mathbf n\ne0$. Dot-product distances use Euclidean coordinates.

derivation.text: In-plane displacement has no normal component.
Substitute the line into the plane.
Convert the perpendicular component to distance.

workedExamples.title: An intersection parameter
workedExamples.problem: Where do line $(x,y,z)=(t,1-t,2t)$ and plane $x+y+z=3$ intersect?
steps: Insert this into the line to obtain $(1,0,2)$.

workedExamples.title: Point-to-plane distance
workedExamples.problem: Find the distance from $(0,0,0)$ to $x+2y+2z=6$.
steps: The plane equation's absolute residual at the origin is 6.

commonMistakes.claim: Nonparallel spatial lines must intersect.
commonMistakes.correction: They can be skew. Check for a common point.

commonMistakes.claim: The equation's constant magnitude is the distance.
commonMistakes.correction: Divide by normal length and account for the chosen point.

practice.problem: Write the line through the origin in direction $\langle1,0,2\rangle$.
solution: $\mathbf r(t)=t\langle1,0,2\rangle$; its vertical coordinate in the horizontal plane stays zero.

practice.problem: Find the plane through $(1,1,1)$ with normal $\langle1,-1,2\rangle$.
solution: Simplification gives $x-y+2z=2$.

practice.problem: Does the horizontal axis in $z=0$ intersect line $(0,1,t)$?
solution: The horizontal axis has second coordinate zero; the other line has second coordinate 1, so no intersection.
Their directions are nonparallel, making them skew.
practice.answer: They neither intersect nor are parallel.

practice.problem: Does $\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf d=0$ ensure the line is not contained in the plane?
practice.hint: Check a point on the line too.
solution: It only makes the direction parallel to the plane.
If the starting point lies in the plane, so does the whole line.

learningCheck.question: If line direction dots nontrivially with plane normal, how many intersections exist?
learningCheck.explanation: Substitution gives a linear parameter equation with nonzero coefficient and one solution.

interactiveVisual.caption: Plane $x+y+z=1$ and line $\mathbf r(t)=(0,0,1)+t(1,1,1)$.
interactiveVisual.prediction: How does the line cross from one side of the plane to the other?

teaching.explain: Substituting a parametrized line into a plane reduces spatial intersection to one equation.

steps.title: Below the plane
steps.observation: The point is below the plane; the signed normal residual is negative.

steps.title: Crossing the plane
steps.observation: The line passes through the plane's center; signed residual is zero.

steps.title: Above the plane
steps.observation: The point is on the opposite side; the residual changes sign.

lessons.title: Quadric surfaces and cross-sections
lessons.subtitle: Understand a surface by slicing it
lessons.concept: Fix one coordinate to obtain a cross-section. Key slices are more reliable than memorized silhouettes.
lessons.intuition: Circles, ellipses, parabolas and hyperbolas in slices reveal the spatial shape.

body.title: Recognizing an ellipsoid
body.text: Three same-sign squared terms equal a positive constant. Find axis intercepts. Fixing one coordinate usually gives an ellipse, possibly a point or empty set.

body.title: Paraboloid versus hyperbolic paraboloid
body.text: For $z=x^2+y^2$, both coordinate slices open upward. For $z=x^2-y^2$, one opens up and the other down, producing a saddle.

body.title: Must a cylinder be circular?
body.text: A missing coordinate means translation invariance in that direction. For example $z=x^2$ extends along the second axis and is a cylinder. Cross terms may require rotated axes; square-term signs alone do not classify them.

formalDefinition.text: Understand a surface by slicing it
conditions: Ellipsoid semiaxes satisfy $a,b,c>0$. These examples use standard forms aligned with principal axes.

derivation.text: Fix height to obtain a plane curve.
Compare perpendicular slices for bending direction.
An absent variable means translation invariance.

workedExamples.title: An ellipsoid slice
workedExamples.problem: Find the slice of $\frac{x^2}4+y^2+\frac{z^2}9=1$ at $z=\frac32$.

workedExamples.title: Recognizing a saddle
workedExamples.problem: Is the origin a minimum of $z=2x^2-y^2$?
steps: Along the other axis, $z=-y^2\le0$; nearby values are both higher and lower.
workedExamples.answer: No; it is a saddle point.

commonMistakes.claim: All level curves are circles.
commonMistakes.correction: Slices may be hyperbolas, lines, empty sets or other shapes.

commonMistakes.claim: A minimum along one direction is a local minimum.
commonMistakes.correction: A multivariable minimum requires no lower nearby values in any direction.

practice.problem: Find the slice radius of $z=x^2+y^2$ at $z=4$.
solution: $x^2+y^2=4$; radius 2.

practice.problem: Find the slice of $x^2+y^2-z^2=1$ at $z=0$.
solution: $x^2+y^2=1$, the unit circle.

practice.problem: Is $y^2+z^2=9$ a sphere?
solution: The first coordinate is arbitrary.
This is a radius-3 cylinder extending along the first axis.

practice.problem: Find the slice of $z=x^2-y^2$ at $z=0$.
solution: Two lines: $y=x$ and $y=-x$.

learningCheck.question: What does a missing first coordinate imply?
choices: Translation invariance along the first axis
learningCheck.explanation: The other coordinates satisfy the equation while the first is free.

interactiveVisual.caption: Vary a parameter in $z=x^2+c y^2$ to move from bowl through cylinder to saddle.
interactiveVisual.prediction: How does reversing one squared term's sign change the surface?

teaching.explain: Fix one coordinate, inspect its slices, then assemble the spatial picture.

steps.title: Bending upward
steps.observation: Both coordinate directions bend upward, forming an elliptic paraboloid.

steps.title: Cylinder
steps.observation: The second coordinate no longer affects height; the surface extends in that direction.

steps.title: Saddle
steps.observation: The coordinate slices bend in opposite directions.

lessons.title: Cylindrical and spherical coordinates
lessons.subtitle: Match coordinates to geometry
lessons.concept: Cylindrical coordinates suit axial shapes; spherical coordinates suit shapes naturally described by distance from the origin.
lessons.intuition: Cylindrical coordinates add height to polar coordinates. Spherical coordinates use distance, azimuth and inclination from the positive vertical axis.
objectives: Convert between three spatial coordinate systems
Identify angle conventions and degenerate points

body.title: Where are angles measured from?
body.text: Azimuth $\theta$ is measured in the horizontal plane from the positive first axis. Inclination $\phi$ is measured downward from the positive vertical axis, from zero to $\pi$.

body.title: Are coordinates unique?
body.text: Adding a full turn changes no point. Azimuth is undefined on the vertical axis, and all angles are nonunique at the origin. These are coordinate degeneracies, not different spatial points.

body.title: Position formulas or volume elements first?
body.text: Understand position geometrically first. Multiple integrals will derive area and volume factors; multiplying three coordinate differentials alone does not give actual volume.

formalDefinition.text: Match coordinates to geometry
conditions: Cylindrical $r\ge0$; spherical $\rho\ge0,0\le\phi\le\pi$. Azimuths differing by full turns are equivalent. Use radians.

derivation.text: Project onto the horizontal plane.
Use distance from the origin and inclination.
Resolve the horizontal radius into components.

workedExamples.title: Reading spherical coordinates
workedExamples.problem: Find spherical coordinates of $(x,y,z)=(1,1,\sqrt2)$.

workedExamples.title: A coordinate surface
workedExamples.problem: What does spherical equation $\phi=\frac\pi3$ describe?
workedExamples.answer: A cone in the upper half-space, including its vertex.

commonMistakes.claim: Every book uses the same symbols for spherical angles.
commonMistakes.correction: Check conventions. Here inclination is measured from the positive vertical axis.

commonMistakes.claim: Cylindrical radius is distance from the origin.
commonMistakes.correction: It is distance from the vertical axis; these agree only at zero height.

practice.problem: Convert cylindrical $(r,\theta,z)=(2,\frac\pi2,-1)$ to Cartesian coordinates.
solution: $x=0,y=2$; height remains $-1$.

practice.problem: What surface is spherical equation $\rho=3$?
solution: Every point is distance 3 from the origin.

practice.problem: Is the azimuth of $(0,0,2)$ unique?
solution: Horizontal radius is zero; every azimuth gives the same point.

practice.problem: Which inclination gives the spherical equator?
practice.hint: Set height zero and distance nonzero.
solution: $\cos\phi=0$, hence $\phi=\frac\pi2$.

learningCheck.question: At zero inclination, where is the point under this convention?
choices: On the positive vertical axis or at the origin
learningCheck.explanation: Inclination is measured from the positive vertical axis.

interactiveVisual.caption: Fix spherical radius $\rho=1.5$ and vary inclination and azimuth. Dashed lines show horizontal projection and origin distance.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Near a pole, does the same azimuth change cover the same distance as at the equator?

teaching.explain: Cylindrical radius measures distance to the axis; spherical radius to the origin. Inclination starts at the positive vertical axis.

steps.title: North pole
steps.observation: The point lies on the positive vertical axis; azimuth does not change it.

steps.title: Equator
steps.observation: Height is zero; horizontal radius equals spherical radius.

steps.title: South pole
steps.observation: The point lies on the negative vertical axis; horizontal radius is zero again.

lessons.title: Vector-valued functions and tangents
lessons.subtitle: One parameter controls a spatial path
lessons.concept: A vector-valued function gives position. Its derivative is instantaneous velocity, pointing along the path.
lessons.intuition: Three single-variable coordinate functions share one parameter. Differentiate components to obtain spatial velocity.
objectives: Find spatial velocity and tangent lines
Recover position from velocity and initial data

body.title: Computing vector limits
body.text: In finite dimensions, compute limits, continuity and derivatives componentwise. Failure in one component prevents the corresponding vector property.

body.title: Why does the derivative give a tangent?
body.text: Displacement divided by elapsed parameter tends to velocity. Nonzero velocity defines a tangent; zero velocity needs separate analysis.

body.title: What does integration give?
body.text: Integrating velocity gives displacement. Add initial position to obtain position; each component has its own constant.

formalDefinition.text: One parameter controls a spatial path
conditions: The tangent formula requires differentiability and nonzero velocity. Integrate components over their stated interval.

derivation.text: Expand the displacement quotient componentwise.
Take limits to obtain velocity.
Use position and nonzero velocity to write the tangent.

workedExamples.title: A helix tangent
workedExamples.problem: Find the tangent of $\mathbf r(t)=\langle\cos t,\sin t,t\rangle$ at time zero.
steps: Velocity $\langle-\sin t,\cos t,1\rangle$ becomes $\langle0,1,1\rangle$ at zero.

workedExamples.title: Recovering position
workedExamples.problem: $\mathbf v(t)=\langle2t,1,-2\rangle,\mathbf r(0)=(1,0,3)$.
steps: Initial position selects the three constants.

commonMistakes.claim: Every spatial curve must be a height graph.
commonMistakes.correction: Closed circles and helices suit parameterization and need not be single-coordinate graphs.

commonMistakes.claim: Zero velocity always means no tangent.
commonMistakes.correction: For example $\mathbf r(t)=(t^3,0,0)$ still lies along the first axis at zero; use an additional limiting argument.

practice.problem: Find the velocity of $\langle t,t^2,t^3\rangle$ at $t=1$.
solution: Velocity is $\langle1,2t,3t^2\rangle$.
Substitution gives $\langle1,2,3\rangle$.

practice.problem: Find the speed of $\mathbf r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t,0)$.
solution: Velocity $\langle-2\sin t,2\cos t,0\rangle$ has constant length 2.

practice.problem: For $\mathbf r(t)=(t^2,t^2,0)$ at zero, can its derivative be used as a nonzero tangent direction?
solution: Velocity vanishes at zero, giving no direction.
The curve lies on line $y=x,z=0$; a separate argument gives the tangent.
practice.answer: The nonzero-velocity formula cannot be used directly.

practice.problem: Is the integration constant in position a scalar?
solution: Each component has one constant.
Together they form a constant vector.

learningCheck.question: Where does velocity point at a regular curve point?
learningCheck.explanation: Velocity is the limit of displacement quotients.

interactiveVisual.caption: $\mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,0.2t)$; arrows show the actual derivative direction. A closed horizontal projection does not make the spatial curve closed.
interactiveVisual.prediction: After one revolution, does the spatial point return to its start?

teaching.explain: Differentiate position's three components and combine them into velocity.

steps.title: Starting point
steps.observation: At the helix's start, the tangent has both horizontal and vertical components.

steps.title: Half a revolution
steps.observation: The point rotates half a turn and rises; its tangent rotates too.

steps.title: One revolution
steps.observation: Horizontal position returns, but height increases, so the spatial path does not close.

lessons.title: Velocity, acceleration and distance
lessons.subtitle: Velocity has direction; speed does not
lessons.concept: Velocity is position's rate of change. Speed is its length. Integrating speed gives distance; integrating velocity gives displacement.
lessons.intuition: A full circle returns to the start but covers nonzero distance. Vector contributions cancel; lengths do not.
objectives: Recover motion from acceleration and initial data

body.title: Does acceleration always increase speed?
body.text: Only its component along velocity directly changes speed. Perpendicular acceleration changes direction; uniform circular motion still accelerates.

body.title: Recovering a trajectory
body.text: Integrate acceleration and use initial velocity. Then integrate velocity and use initial position. Both sets of data matter.

body.title: Why does length integrate speed?
body.text: A short travel length is approximately speed times elapsed time. Accumulate it along a piecewise smooth curve; retracing counts again.

formalDefinition.text: Velocity has direction; speed does not
formalDefinition.latex: \mathbf v=\mathbf r\prime,\quad\mathbf a=\mathbf r^{\prime\prime},\quad L=\int_\alpha^\beta\|\mathbf r\prime(t)\|dt,\quad\Delta\mathbf r=\int_\alpha^\beta\mathbf v(t)dt
conditions: Arc length uses a piecewise continuously differentiable path. Acceleration requires a second derivative. Compare displacement and distance over the same interval.

derivation.text: Approximate short displacement by velocity times time.
Take lengths and accumulate distance.
Differentiate speed squared to analyze acceleration's effect.

workedExamples.title: Distance along a helix
workedExamples.problem: Find the distance covered by $\mathbf r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t,3t)$ over one revolution.
steps: The time interval has length $2\pi$; integrate the constant speed.

workedExamples.title: Projectile position
steps: Integrate again and use initial position to obtain $(t,2t,1+3t-t^2)$.
workedExamples.answer: $\mathbf r(t)=(t,2t,1+3t-t^2)$; interpret only while the model is valid.

commonMistakes.claim: Nonzero acceleration always increases speed.
commonMistakes.correction: It may change direction alone.

commonMistakes.claim: Distance equals displacement magnitude.
commonMistakes.correction: Distance is generally larger; changes of direction cause displacement cancellation.

practice.problem: A radius-3 circle is traversed at one radian per unit time. Find speed.
solution: The derivative of $\mathbf r=(3\cos t,3\sin t,0)$ has length 3.

practice.problem: Find displacement and distance over one unit-circle revolution.
practice.hint: Integrate the vector and its length separately.
solution: Matching endpoints give zero displacement.
Speed is 1; distance is $2\pi$.

practice.problem: Given $\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a=0$ and nonzero velocity, find the instantaneous derivative of speed.
solution: $2v v\prime=2\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a=0$; since $v>0$, obtain $v\prime=0$.

practice.problem: Are zero velocity and constant speed equivalent?
practice.hint: Use uniform circular motion as a counterexample.
solution: It has positive constant speed while velocity's direction changes.

learningCheck.question: What is acceleration in uniform circular motion?
choices: Perpendicular to velocity and toward the center
learningCheck.explanation: Tangential acceleration is zero; the normal component turns the path.

interactiveVisual.caption: $\mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,0)$; green denotes velocity, blue acceleration.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Why is acceleration nonzero when speed is constant?

teaching.explain: Integrating velocity gives displacement; integrating its length gives distance without cancellation.

steps.title: Start moving
steps.observation: Velocity is tangent to the circle; acceleration points inward.

steps.title: A quarter revolution
steps.observation: Velocity rotates while retaining its length.

steps.title: A full revolution
steps.observation: Displacement is zero, while distance equals the circumference.

lessons.title: Arc-length parameters and curvature
lessons.subtitle: Separate turning from travel speed
lessons.concept: Curvature measures tangent-direction change per unit distance. It describes the curve's shape.
lessons.intuition: The same bend is equally curved at any travel speed. Measuring tangent change by arc length removes speed's effect.

body.title: The unit tangent
body.text: Normalize nonzero velocity to obtain $\mathbf T$. The length of its derivative with respect to arc length is curvature.

body.title: Decomposing acceleration
body.text: Tangential acceleration changes speed; normal acceleration has magnitude curvature times speed squared. Nonzero curvature defines principal normal and binormal.

body.title: Is torsion required here?
body.text: This volume focuses on length and curvature. Torsion measures departure from the osculating plane and belongs to differential geometry; it is unnecessary for these integral theorems.

formalDefinition.text: Separate turning from travel speed
formalDefinition.latex: \mathbf T=\frac{\mathbf r\prime}{\|\mathbf r\prime\|},\quad\kappa=\left\|\frac{d\mathbf T}{ds}\right\|=\frac{\|\mathbf r\prime\times\mathbf r^{\prime\prime}\|}{\|\mathbf r\prime\|^3},\quad\mathbf a=v\prime\mathbf T+v^2\kappa\mathbf N
conditions: The curve is twice continuously differentiable with nonzero velocity. $\mathbf N$ also requires nonzero curvature. Arc length is monotone on a regular interval.

derivation.text: Arc length changes at the speed.
Changes in unit tangent are perpendicular to it.
Differentiate velocity's magnitude and direction separately.

workedExamples.title: Curvature of a circle
workedExamples.problem: Find the curvature of a radius-4 circle.
steps: Unit arc length produces angular change $1/4$.
The velocity-acceleration cross-product formula gives the same result.

workedExamples.title: Helix curvature
workedExamples.problem: Find the curvature of $\mathbf r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t,t)$.
steps: Velocity length is $\sqrt5$; acceleration length is 2, and they are perpendicular.
The cross-product length is $2\sqrt5$; divide by $5\sqrt5$.

commonMistakes.claim: Faster travel means larger curvature.
commonMistakes.correction: Regular reparameterization preserves curvature. Normal acceleration, instead, scales with speed squared.

commonMistakes.claim: A straight line's principal normal is uniquely given by the formula.
commonMistakes.correction: A straight line has zero curvature, so this normalization does not define a principal normal.

practice.problem: Find the curvature of a radius-2 circle.
solution: Arc length $ds$ produces turn angle $ds/2$.

practice.problem: Find the curvature of $\mathbf r(t)=(t,0,0)$.
solution: The cross product vanishes and speed is 1, so curvature is zero.

practice.problem: If speed doubles on the same circle, what happens to normal acceleration?
solution: By $a_N=\kappa v^2$, it quadruples.

practice.problem: Can the cross-product formula be used directly when $\mathbf r\prime(t_0)=0$?
solution: The speed-cubed denominator is zero.
Choose a regular parameter or analyze separately; division is invalid.

learningCheck.question: If the same path is traveled at twice the speed, how does curvature change?
learningCheck.explanation: Curvature depends on shape and has units of reciprocal length.

interactiveVisual.caption: Vary the radius to compare unit tangent, principal normal and curvature, with equal coordinate scaling.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Does a larger radius turn more or less per unit distance?

teaching.explain: Tangent turning per distance gives curvature independently of speed.

steps.title: Small radius
steps.observation: The circle is tighter; curvature is 2.

steps.title: Unit radius
steps.observation: Curvature is 1.

steps.title: Large radius
steps.observation: The bend is gentler; curvature is one-half.

lessons.title: Multivariable functions and level sets
lessons.subtitle: Assign one value to each input position
lessons.concept: A two-variable function assigns height to each allowed planar position. A contour joins positions with the same height.
lessons.intuition: Color maps and contours encode heights. A surface shows shape; contours make directions easier to read.

body.title: Finding the domain
body.text: Require nonnegative radicands, positive logarithm arguments and nonzero denominators. Intersect the conditions to find a planar or spatial region.

body.title: Graph versus contour
body.text: A graph displays output as height. A contour stays in the input plane with output fixed. Contours of different values cannot intersect.

body.title: Displaying three-variable functions
body.text: Three input coordinates already fill space. Use level surfaces or slices for output; the four-dimensional graph is not an ordinary spatial surface.

formalDefinition.text: Assign one value to each input position
conditions: The function is single-valued on its domain. Level sets may be empty, points, curves or regions, and need not be smooth.

derivation.text: Specify allowed inputs.
Fix the output to obtain a level set.
Use coordinate slices to inspect height changes.

workedExamples.title: A radical's domain
workedExamples.problem: Find the domain of $f(x,y)=\sqrt{9-x^2-y^2}$.
steps: The radicand must be nonnegative, giving $x^2+y^2\le9$.
Zero radicand is allowed on the boundary.

workedExamples.title: A contour
workedExamples.problem: Find the height-4 contour of $f(x,y)=x^2+4y^2$.

commonMistakes.claim: The graph of a two-variable function is a planar region.
commonMistakes.correction: The planar region is its domain; the graph is usually a spatial surface.

commonMistakes.claim: Dense contours always mean high elevation.
commonMistakes.correction: With equal contour intervals and scale, density indicates rapid change, not absolute height.

practice.problem: Find the domain of $\ln(y-x^2)$.
practice.hint: The logarithm's input must be strictly positive.
solution: $y-x^2>0$; exclude the boundary parabola.

practice.problem: Find the zero-level set of $x^2+y^2$.
solution: Both coordinates must vanish.

practice.problem: Can contours of different heights intersect?
solution: An intersection would assign two different outputs to one input.

practice.problem: What does a level surface of a three-variable temperature function represent?
solution: It contains every point at the specified temperature.
practice.answer: The set of positions with the same temperature.

learningCheck.question: Is $x^2+y^2=0$ a circular curve?
learningCheck.explanation: Only the origin satisfies it. Level sets need not be regular curves.

interactiveVisual.caption: Surface $z=x^2+y^2$ with a fixed-first-coordinate slice; the projection marks corresponding inputs.
interactiveVisual.prediction: When moving in the plane, which coordinates are inputs and which is output?

teaching.explain: The domain lies in the input plane; the graph raises output into height, while contours retain equal-height positions.

steps.title: Central slice
steps.observation: The slice passes through the bowl's bottom, with minimum height zero.

steps.title: Shift the slice
steps.observation: The entire slice rises.

steps.title: A farther slice
steps.observation: The minimum height is 1.

lessons.title: Multivariable limits and continuity
lessons.subtitle: Every approach must lead to the same value
lessons.concept: A multivariable limit controls every approach within the domain. Two conflicting paths disprove it; finitely many agreeing paths do not prove it.
lessons.intuition: Approach one junction by different roads. Conflicting limiting heights prevent a common limit.

body.title: What becomes small?
body.text: Euclidean input distance becomes small, forcing output error small. The chosen radius must work for all allowed directions.

body.title: What can path tests establish?
body.text: Two legitimate paths with different limits disprove existence. Finitely many agreeing paths do not suffice; even all straight lines may miss a curved-path failure.

body.title: Proving existence
body.text: Bound output error by a quantity depending only on distance and tending to zero. Continuity additionally requires agreement with the value at the point.

formalDefinition.text: Every approach must lead to the same value
conditions: Approach within the domain toward an accumulation point. Continuity also requires the target in the domain and $L=f(\mathbf a)$.

derivation.text: Vary straight-line slope to inspect path values.
Two conflicting path limits give a contradiction.
A uniform estimate proves the limit in another example.

workedExamples.title: Conflicting paths
workedExamples.problem: Does $\frac{xy}{x^2+y^2}$ have a limit at the origin?
steps: Along the first axis, the function is zero.
Along $y=x$, it equals $1/2$; the limits conflict.

workedExamples.title: A uniform squeeze
workedExamples.problem: Find the origin limit of $\frac{x^2y}{x^2+y^2}$.

commonMistakes.claim: Matching limits on both axes prove existence.
commonMistakes.correction: Only two paths were checked; control every direction together.

commonMistakes.claim: A limit requires a defined value at the point.
commonMistakes.correction: Limits concern nearby values; the target itself may be outside the domain.

practice.problem: Does $\frac{x^2-y^2}{x^2+y^2}$ have a limit at the origin?
solution: The first gives 1; the second gives $-1$, a contradiction.

practice.problem: Prove $x^2y\to0$.
solution: Set $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$; then $|x^2y|\le r^3$.
Let $r\to0$; the right side tends to zero.

practice.problem: If every straight-line limit is zero, must the full limit be zero?
solution: $\frac{x^2y}{x^4+y^2}$ tends to zero along each line through the origin.
But along $y=x^2$, it is constantly $1/2$.

practice.problem: Can assigning an origin value make $\frac{xy}{x^2+y^2}$ continuous?
solution: The path conflict is independent of the origin's value.
No assigned value can repair a missing limit.

learningCheck.question: Two path limits differ. What follows?
learningCheck.explanation: One limit must apply along every legitimate path.

interactiveVisual.caption: $f(x,y)=\frac{xy}{x^2+y^2}$ approaches the origin at direction angle $\theta$. Finite paths illustrate a counterexample, not existence.
interactiveVisual.prediction: As distance shrinks, do values from different directions merge?

teaching.explain: Two conflicting paths disprove a limit; proving one requires an estimate valid in all directions.

steps.title: Along the first axis
steps.observation: The path height is always zero.

steps.title: Along the diagonal
steps.observation: Height is one-half, unlike on the axis.

steps.title: Look closer
steps.observation: The directional difference remains even at small distance; zooming does not remove it.

lessons.title: Partial and higher-order derivatives
lessons.subtitle: Change one input at a time
lessons.concept: A partial derivative measures instantaneous change in one variable while all others stay fixed.
lessons.intuition: Slice a surface in a coordinate direction and differentiate that single-variable curve. Different directions may have different slopes.
objectives: Compute first and mixed partial derivatives
Recognize what partial derivatives cannot guarantee

body.title: What happens to other variables?
body.text: Hold the second variable constant when differentiating in the first, then reverse roles. A partial derivative describes one slice, not a uniform approximation in every direction.

body.title: Can mixed derivatives be exchanged?
body.text: Continuity of the second mixed derivatives nearby is sufficient. Without suitable conditions, do not interchange the order by notation alone.

body.title: Do existing partials imply smoothness?
body.text: They need not even imply continuity, let alone differentiability. Normal axis slices can hide diagonal anomalies.

formalDefinition.text: Change one input at a time
conditions: Difference quotients stay within the domain. Continuous second mixed partials near the point suffice to interchange them.

derivation.text: Fix one variable.
Differentiate the resulting one-variable slice.
Differentiate that partial-derivative function again.

workedExamples.title: Separate derivatives
workedExamples.problem: Find both partials of $f=x^2y+\sin y$.

workedExamples.title: Checking mixed derivatives
workedExamples.problem: Find both mixed partials of $f=x^2y^3$.
steps: $f_x=2xy^3$; differentiating in the second variable gives $6xy^2$.
Reverse order also gives $6xy^2$. Polynomial smoothness meets the continuity condition.

commonMistakes.claim: The other variable has derivative one.
commonMistakes.correction: It is fixed here, so its derivative is zero.

commonMistakes.claim: Existing partial derivatives imply continuity.
commonMistakes.correction: Axis checks are insufficient; the multivariable limit may fail.

practice.problem: Find $f_x$ for $f=e^{xy}$.
practice.hint: The inner first-variable derivative is the second variable.
solution: The chain rule gives $f_x=ye^{xy}$.

practice.problem: For $f=x^2+3xy+y^2$ at $(1,2)$, find $f_y$.
practice.hint: Differentiate first, then substitute the point.
solution: Substitution gives 7.

practice.problem: For $g=\frac{xy}{x^2+y^2}$, extended by zero at the origin, find both origin partials.
solution: The function vanishes on both axes, so both quotients are zero.
Its diagonal values do not tend to zero, so continuity fails.
practice.answer: Both partials are zero, yet the function is discontinuous.

practice.problem: Can mixed partials always be interchanged?
solution: Continuous second mixed partials nearby suffice.
Otherwise calculate both orders or give another justification.

learningCheck.question: When differentiating $x^2y$ in its first variable, how is the second treated?
learningCheck.explanation: Partial differentiation fixes all other independent variables.

interactiveVisual.caption: Surface $z=x^2+y^2$ at $(a,b,a^2+b^2)$, with coordinate slices and tangents. Gold follows the first direction, blue the second; slopes are $2a$, $2b$.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Does the first-direction slope stay the same at different points?

teaching.explain: A partial derivative changes one input alone; the other is fixed for that calculation.

steps.title: First direction
steps.instruction: Use $a=-1,b=0$ and inspect the gold tangent.
steps.observation: The first partial is $-2$, the second zero. They belong to distinct slices.

steps.title: Change the second coordinate only
steps.observation: The first partial stays $-2$, while the second becomes $2$; it is not always zero.

steps.title: Compare at one point
steps.observation: At this point the first slope is $1$, the second $-1$. Each requires holding the other variable fixed.

lessons.title: Differentiability, tangent planes and error
lessons.subtitle: Can one plane predict every small displacement?
lessons.concept: Differentiability means one linear expression explains the increment, with remainder negligible relative to displacement length.
lessons.intuition: A tangent plane must approximate all nearby directions, not merely match two coordinate tangents.
objectives: Construct tangent planes and linear approximations

body.title: What goes beyond partial derivatives?
body.text: Partials test coordinate directions. Differentiability requires uniformly smaller-than-first-order error in every direction. It implies continuity; partials alone do not.

body.title: A practical sufficient condition
body.text: Continuous partial derivatives in a neighborhood guarantee differentiability. This is not necessary, so failure does not prove nondifferentiability.

body.title: Approximation versus equality
body.text: The tangent plane gives first-order approximation. Bound actual error separately; do not assume accuracy far from the center.

formalDefinition.text: Can one plane predict every small displacement?
conditions: Little $o$ means remainder divided by displacement length tends to zero. Tangent-plane approximation requires differentiability, guaranteed by continuous partials nearby.

derivation.text: Define the linear model's remainder.
Compare it with displacement length.
Expand the sum of squares directly to check.

workedExamples.title: A tangent plane
workedExamples.problem: Find the tangent plane of $f=x^2+y^2$ at $(1,-1)$.

workedExamples.title: Approximation and error
workedExamples.problem: Use origin linearization to approximate $f(0.1,0.2)$, with $f=1+x+y+x^2+y^2$.
steps: The actual value is $1.35$; error $0.05$ is exactly the sum of squares.

commonMistakes.claim: Existing partials guarantee a tangent-plane approximation.
commonMistakes.correction: Establish differentiability first; partials only suggest a candidate linear model.

commonMistakes.claim: A remainder tending to zero proves differentiability.
commonMistakes.correction: It must tend to zero after division by displacement length, a stronger requirement than continuity.

practice.problem: What is the linearization error for $f=3x-2y+1$?
practice.hint: The function is already a plane.
solution: The linear model equals the function exactly.

practice.problem: For $f=x^2+y^2$ at the origin, find remainder divided by distance.
solution: Remainder $r^2$ divided by $r>0$ gives $r$.
This tends to zero, proving differentiability.

practice.problem: Is $f=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ differentiable at the origin?
solution: The slice is $|x|$, without an origin derivative.
Therefore the original function is not differentiable.

practice.problem: Do discontinuous partials always imply nondifferentiability?
solution: Continuous partials are sufficient.
If that condition fails, the remainder definition may still apply; do not reject differentiability automatically.

learningCheck.question: For a differentiable function, what does remainder divided by displacement length approach?
learningCheck.explanation: The error beyond the linear term must be negligible compared with distance.

interactiveVisual.caption: The tangent plane of $f=x^2+y^2$ at $(0.5,0.5)$; along diagonal displacement $(h,h)$, compare exact and normalized errors.
interactiveVisual.prediction: If displacement shrinks tenfold, about how much does quadratic error shrink?

teaching.explain: Subtract the linear prediction and divide by displacement length. Differentiability means this ratio tends to zero.

steps.title: Larger displacement
steps.observation: A visible quadratic error separates bowl and tangent plane.

steps.title: Reduce displacement
steps.observation: Error shrinks faster than distance.

steps.title: Approach the center
steps.observation: The remainder-to-distance ratio keeps approaching zero; calculations retain finite precision.

lessons.title: The multivariable chain rule and implicit functions
lessons.subtitle: Add contributions from every changing input
lessons.concept: When a quantity depends on several intermediate variables, sum the products of local rates along every dependency path.
lessons.intuition: Along a mountain path, both eastward and northward motion change height. Add their contributions.
objectives: Compute total change along parameter paths
Find implicit derivatives at regular points

body.title: Why add contributions?
body.text: The linear increment is a sum of coordinate contributions. Substitute each coordinate's parameter change into that sum.

body.title: Several input parameters
body.text: Track each input's paths separately, forming a derivative matrix. Matrix multiplication organizes these sums.

body.title: Implicit differentiation
body.text: If $F(x,y)=0$ and $F_y\ne0$, continuous partials nearby allow the second coordinate locally as a differentiable function of the first. Differentiate the identity. Do not use the quotient when its denominator vanishes.

formalDefinition.text: Add contributions from every changing input
conditions: The outer function is differentiable at the path point and inner functions differentiable. The implicit-function conclusion requires $F$ continuously differentiable nearby and $F_y\ne0$.

derivation.text: Write the outer function's linear increment.
Divide by the time increment and take limits.
Differentiate the implicit identity.

workedExamples.title: Differentiating along a path
workedExamples.problem: Given $f=x^2y,x=t,y=t^2$, find the derivative along the path.
steps: Substitution gives $4t^3$; check by substituting $f=t^4$ first.

workedExamples.title: An implicit slope
workedExamples.problem: Find the slope of ellipse $x^2+4y^2=8$ at $(2,1)$.
steps: $F_x=2x,F_y=8y$; the denominator is 8 at that point.

commonMistakes.claim: Only one changing direction contributes to the chain rule.
commonMistakes.correction: Every input varying with the parameter contributes.

commonMistakes.claim: A zero implicit denominator means the derivative is infinity.
commonMistakes.correction: The formula fails; inspect vertical tangency or more serious degeneracy.

practice.problem: Given $f=x+y,x=t^2,y=\sin t$, find the rate at time zero.
solution: $2t+\cos t$ equals 1 at zero.

practice.problem: Find the rate of $f=x^2+y^2$ along $x=\cos t,y=\sin t$.
solution: The function is constantly 1 along the path, so its derivative is zero.
The two chain-rule contributions cancel.

practice.problem: For $x^2+y^2=1$ at $(1,0)$, can you use $-x/y$?
solution: The denominator vanishes; the second coordinate is not locally differentiable as a function of the first here.
The circle has a vertical tangent.

practice.problem: Given $F(x,y,z)=0,F_z\ne0$, find local $z_x$.
practice.hint: Fix the second variable and differentiate the identity in the first.
solution: $F_x+F_z z_x=0$.
This gives $z_x=-F_x/F_z$.

learningCheck.question: What is the rate when moving along a contour?
learningCheck.explanation: Constant function value makes the chain-rule sum zero.

interactiveVisual.caption: Move on the unit circle on bowl $z=x^2+y^2$; observe the two coordinate contributions cancel.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Can the total rate vanish when both partials are nonzero?

teaching.explain: Find how each intermediate variable changes, then add its contribution.

steps.title: Path start
steps.observation: Start at $(1,0)$, at height 1.

steps.title: Path midpoint
steps.observation: Height stays 1 along the unit circle.

steps.title: Path endpoint
steps.observation: Position and direction change while the total height rate remains zero.

lessons.title: Directional derivatives and gradients
lessons.subtitle: Find the steepest ascent direction
lessons.concept: For a differentiable function, the gradient encodes every directional first-order rate in one vector.
lessons.intuition: The gradient points steepest uphill. Perpendicular directions have zero first-order height change and lie tangent to contours.
objectives: Compute directional rates and steepest directions
Find level-surface tangent planes from gradients

body.title: Why normalize the direction?
body.text: Directional derivatives measure change per unit distance. Nonunit vectors mix in travel speed; time-path derivatives instead use the actual velocity.

body.title: How steep is the steepest ascent?
body.text: A dot product is at most the product of lengths. A unit direction aligned with the gradient gives its length; the opposite gives its negative.

body.title: Why normal to a level surface?
body.text: A tangent movement preserves function value, so its dot product with the gradient vanishes. A zero gradient cannot specify a unique normal.

formalDefinition.text: Find the steepest ascent direction
formalDefinition.latex: D_{\mathbf u}f=\nabla f\cdot\mathbf u,\quad\|\mathbf u\|=1,\quad\nabla f=\langle f_x,f_y,f_z\rangle
conditions: The dot-product formula requires differentiability. Unit directions give change per unit distance. A regular level-surface normal requires nonzero gradient.

derivation.text: Apply the chain rule along a straight path.
Its velocity is the unit direction.
Bound the dot product to find steepest ascent.

workedExamples.title: A specified direction
workedExamples.problem: For $f=x^2+2y^2$ at $(1,1)$, find the derivative along $\langle3,4\rangle$.
steps: The gradient is $\langle2,4\rangle$; normalize the direction to $\langle3/5,4/5\rangle$.

workedExamples.title: A level-surface normal
workedExamples.problem: Find the tangent plane of $x^2+y^2+z^2=9$ at $(1,2,2)$.

commonMistakes.claim: Directions need no normalization.
commonMistakes.correction: Change per unit distance requires a unit vector.

commonMistakes.claim: Zero gradient means no higher-order change.
commonMistakes.correction: First-order rates vanish, but second- or higher-order change may remain.

practice.problem: Find the maximum directional derivative of $f=3x+4y$.
solution: Gradient $(3,4)$ has length 5.

practice.problem: For $f=x^2+y^2$ at $(1,0)$, find the derivative in the positive second-axis direction.
solution: Gradient $(2,0)$ dotted with $(0,1)$ is zero.

practice.problem: A contour-tangent directional derivative vanishes. Is the function constant along that whole straight line?
practice.hint: Is first-order information a global statement?
solution: Only the first-order rate at that point is zero.
On a bowl at $(1,0)$, a straight move along the second direction still increases height quadratically.

practice.problem: Does the zero origin gradient of $f=x^2-y^2$ prove a minimum?
solution: Values on the first axis are nonnegative; on the second, nonpositive.
Nearby values lie both above and below, making a saddle.

learningCheck.question: A unit direction is perpendicular to the gradient. What is its directional derivative?
learningCheck.explanation: The dot product is zero, but second-order changes may remain.

interactiveVisual.caption: At $(1,0,1)$, the bowl's gradient points along the positive first axis. Rotate a unit direction and compare slopes.
interactiveVisual.prediction: What angle separates steepest ascent from zero first-order change?

teaching.explain: Project the gradient onto a unit direction to obtain that direction's first-order rate.

steps.title: Aligned
steps.observation: Alignment gives the maximum directional derivative.

steps.title: Perpendicular
steps.observation: The directional derivative vanishes; only the first-order rate is zero.

steps.title: Opposing
steps.observation: The derivative is negative, giving steepest descent.

lessons.title: Second-order Taylor models
lessons.subtitle: Add the bending a tangent plane misses
lessons.concept: Second-order Taylor polynomials record directional curvature and interactions beyond the tangent plane.
lessons.intuition: Linear terms describe slope; quadratic terms describe bowls, saddles and mixed-direction coupling.
objectives: Check mixed terms and remainder hypotheses

body.title: What is the Hessian?
body.text: The matrix of second partial derivatives. It is symmetric when those derivatives are continuous. Multiplying by displacement on both sides produces a scalar quadratic form.

body.title: Why do mixed terms appear twice?
body.text: The two differentiation orders contribute separately; the overall one-half compensates. Do not omit a contribution again.

body.title: Controlling the remainder
body.text: Continuous second derivatives give a remainder negligible relative to squared distance. Bounded third derivatives near the connecting segment give a cubic bound via one-variable Taylor.

formalDefinition.text: Add the bending a tangent plane misses
conditions: Evaluate coefficients at the center. The function is twice continuously differentiable nearby; explicit cubic bounds require third-order hypotheses.

derivation.text: Restrict the function to the displacement line segment.
Apply the chain rule twice to obtain the quadratic form.
Apply one-variable Taylor to the segment parameter.

workedExamples.title: An exponential model
workedExamples.problem: Find the second-order polynomial of $f=e^{x+y}$ at the origin.

workedExamples.title: An explicit error
workedExamples.problem: Use this model for $e^{0.1+0.1}$, with a bound.
steps: The exponential remainder along the segment is at most $e^{0.2}(0.2)^3/6<0.00163$.

commonMistakes.claim: Second-order terms contain only pure squares.
commonMistakes.correction: Mixed terms matter and can change diagonal bending.

commonMistakes.claim: The Taylor polynomial equals the original function.
commonMistakes.correction: It is usually a local approximation; retain the remainder in exact equalities.

practice.problem: Find the origin Hessian of $x^2+3xy+2y^2$.
solution: Pure second partials are 2 and 4; mixed partials are 3.

practice.problem: Find the second-order origin polynomial of $\sin(x+y)$.
practice.hint: Sine's second derivative at zero vanishes.
solution: Constant zero; linear term $x+y$; every quadratic term vanishes.

practice.problem: In the origin second-order expansion of $e^{x+y}$, what is the coefficient of $xy$?
practice.hint: Expand the square or count both contributions.
solution: $\frac12(2xy)=xy$; coefficient 1.

practice.problem: Do second partials existing at one point suffice for this remainder theorem?
solution: The theorem requires twice continuous differentiability nearby.
Values at a single point do not establish that sufficient condition.
practice.answer: Not enough to apply it directly.

learningCheck.question: Where does a second-order mixed term come from?
learningCheck.explanation: Each chain-rule differentiation order contributes.

interactiveVisual.caption: Model $f=e^{x+y}$ to second order at zero; compare exact and approximate heights along $(h,h)$.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Must the second-order model be exact away from its center?

teaching.explain: Join the center to the target by a line and apply single-variable Taylor along it.

steps.title: Larger displacement
steps.observation: The quadratic approximation still has visible remainder.

steps.title: Small displacement
steps.observation: The quadratic model lies closer than the tangent plane to the exponential surface.

steps.title: Smaller displacement
steps.observation: The cubic bound decreases further; exact equality still needs a remainder.

lessons.title: Critical points and the second-derivative test
lessons.subtitle: After zero gradient, inspect bending
lessons.concept: A differentiable interior extremum must have zero gradient. Second-order shape distinguishes a bowl bottom, top or saddle.
lessons.intuition: Zero slope looks flat to first order. Inspect whether nearby directions all rise, all fall or do both.
objectives: Find stationary points and apply the Hessian test

body.title: What counts as a critical point?
body.text: Candidates include domain points where the gradient vanishes or does not exist. The second-order test applies only to sufficiently smooth stationary points.

body.title: What does the determinant test?
body.text: A positive-definite Hessian bends up in every direction; negative-definite bends down; indefinite gives a saddle. The two-variable discriminant is its determinant.

body.title: What if the determinant is zero?
body.text: The quadratic term may be insufficient. Inspect higher terms or use the definition; do not declare a saddle automatically.

formalDefinition.text: After zero gradient, inspect bending
conditions: The function is twice continuously differentiable near a zero-gradient point. The conclusions give strict local extrema; $D=0$ is inconclusive.

derivation.text: An interior extremum restricts to an extremum on each coordinate line.
The quadratic model controls signs of sufficiently small displacements.
Completing the square gives the two-dimensional criterion.

workedExamples.title: A bowl with a mixed term
workedExamples.problem: Classify the origin of $f=x^2+xy+y^2$.
workedExamples.answer: A strict local minimum, also the global minimum.

workedExamples.title: A degenerate minimum
workedExamples.problem: Classify the origin of $f=x^4+y^4$.
steps: All origin second partials vanish; the test is inconclusive.
The function is nonnegative and vanishes only at the origin.

commonMistakes.claim: Zero gradient always implies a minimum.
commonMistakes.correction: Maxima and saddles can also have zero gradient.

commonMistakes.claim: Zero determinant rules out an extremum.
commonMistakes.correction: It only makes this test inconclusive.

practice.problem: Classify the origin of $f=-x^2-2y^2$.
solution: Every nearby nonorigin value is negative; the origin is zero.

practice.problem: Classify the origin of $f=xy$.
solution: Along $y=x$, the value is $x^2$; along $y=-x$, it is $-x^2$.

practice.problem: The origin Hessian of $f=x^4-y^4$ is zero. Classify it.
solution: Values rise along the first axis and fall along the second.

practice.problem: Can the second-derivative test directly classify boundary extrema?
solution: Boundary constraints may invalidate even the zero-gradient necessary condition.
Analyze the boundary separately.

learningCheck.question: What does $D=0$ imply?
learningCheck.explanation: Higher-order terms or direct comparison may decide.

interactiveVisual.caption: Vary one Hessian coefficient in $f=x^2+c y^2$ to see a bowl, degenerate valley and saddle.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Why can the origin change from minimum to saddle while its gradient stays zero?

teaching.explain: Zero gradient selects candidates. Opposite quadratic signs in different directions give a saddle.

steps.title: Positive definite
steps.observation: Both directions rise; the origin is a bowl bottom.

steps.title: Degenerate
steps.observation: The second direction is flat; the test gives no strict minimum.

steps.title: Indefinite
steps.observation: The second direction falls; the origin is a saddle.

lessons.title: Global extrema on closed regions
lessons.subtitle: Check interior, boundary and corners
lessons.concept: A continuous function on a nonempty closed bounded region attains its maximum and minimum. Compare all candidates.
lessons.intuition: A room's highest point may be in the interior, along a wall or at a corner. Interior stationary points alone miss the edges.

body.title: What guarantees attainment?
body.text: A nonempty closed bounded subset of Euclidean space is compact. Continuous functions on it attain extrema. Missing hypotheses require another argument.

body.title: Analyzing boundaries
body.text: Parametrize each boundary piece as a one-variable problem. Include endpoints, corners and nondifferentiable points, then compare with interior candidates.

body.title: Unbounded regions
body.text: Growth at infinity sometimes reduces the problem to a bounded region. Sometimes a supremum or infimum is never attained. Distinguish a maximum from an upper bound.

formalDefinition.text: Check interior, boundary and corners
formalDefinition.latex: \min_D f,\max_D f\in f(D)\quad\text{if }D\ne\varnothing\text{ is compact and }f\text{ is continuous}
conditions: Existence here requires a nonempty closed bounded domain and continuity. Calculations must also handle boundary pieces and nondifferentiable points.

derivation.text: Smooth interior candidates have zero gradient.
Restrict each boundary piece to one variable.
Compare all feasible candidate values.

workedExamples.title: Squared distance on a disk
workedExamples.problem: Find extrema of $f=(x-1)^2+y^2$ on $x^2+y^2\le4$.
steps: On the boundary set $(x,y)=(2\cos t,2\sin t)$; the function is $5-4\cos t$, with maximum 9.

workedExamples.title: An open-domain warning
workedExamples.problem: Does $f=x+y$ have a maximum and minimum on $0<x<1,0<y<1$?
steps: Values lie strictly between zero and 2.
They approach endpoint values without attaining them.

commonMistakes.claim: Continuity guarantees extrema on every domain.
commonMistakes.correction: Domain hypotheses or another argument are needed.

commonMistakes.claim: Stop after finding interior stationary points.
commonMistakes.correction: Global extrema may occur on boundaries or corners.

practice.problem: Find the maximum of $f=x+y$ on the closed unit square.
solution: Both coordinates equal 1, giving 2.

practice.problem: Find the minimum of $f=x^2+y^2$ on the closed radius-3 disk.
solution: It is in the domain and the function is nonnegative.

practice.problem: Does $f=x$ have a maximum over the plane?
practice.hint: Travel outward along the positive first axis.
solution: The first coordinate and function value are unbounded.

practice.problem: Must an extremal corner on a closed region have zero gradient?
solution: Allowed directions at a corner are restricted; interior Fermat conditions do not apply directly.
Include corners separately.

learningCheck.question: Should global-extremum candidates include the boundary?
learningCheck.explanation: Interior necessary conditions cannot replace boundary checks.

interactiveVisual.caption: Compare values at target $(1,0)$ inside the disk and at a moving boundary point.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Must the boundary minimum be the disk's global minimum?

teaching.explain: Establish attainment, then compare interior, boundary and corner candidates together.

steps.title: Nearest boundary point
steps.observation: The radius-2 boundary point is squared distance 1 from $(1,0)$.

steps.title: Side boundary
steps.observation: Its function value is 5.

steps.title: Farthest boundary point
steps.observation: The boundary value reaches 9; the global minimum remains inside.

lessons.title: Lagrange multipliers and constrained extrema
lessons.subtitle: At an optimum, feasible directions have zero first-order change
lessons.concept: On a smooth equality constraint, an extremal objective gradient is normally parallel to the constraint gradient. Multipliers express that alignment.
lessons.intuition: If the objective gradient has a feasible tangent component, moving one way still increases the objective. At a regular extremal candidate, normals align.

body.title: Why not set the objective gradient to zero?
body.text: The constraint restricts directions. The objective can rise in forbidden directions while no allowed direction increases it.

body.title: What points may be missed?
body.text: A zero constraint gradient can invalidate the multiplier condition. Check singular points separately, as well as boundaries, inequalities and escape to infinity.

body.title: Multiple constraints
body.text: With independent constraint gradients, the objective gradient is their linear combination. Otherwise inspect degeneracy and potentially missed candidates.

formalDefinition.text: At an optimum, feasible directions have zero first-order change
formalDefinition.latex:
abla f=\lambda
abla g,\quad g=c;\qquad 
abla f=\lambda
abla g+\mu
abla h
conditions: Functions and constraints are continuously differentiable nearby. A single constraint needs nonzero gradient; multiple constraints need independent gradients. Solutions are only candidates: compare them and check omissions.

derivation.text: Feasible tangents are perpendicular to the constraint gradient.
An extremum has zero first-order change along every feasible tangent.
The two normals are therefore parallel.

workedExamples.title: A linear objective on a circle
workedExamples.problem: Find extrema of $f=2x+y$ subject to $x^2+y^2=5$.
steps: The constraint gives $(2,1)$ and $(-2,-1)$, with objective values plus and minus 5.

workedExamples.title: A product on a sphere
workedExamples.problem: Maximize $xy$ subject to $x^2+y^2+z^2=2$.
steps: Equality occurs at $(1,1,0)$ and $(-1,-1,0)$, checking the multiplier candidates.

commonMistakes.claim: Every multiplier solution is an extremum.
commonMistakes.correction: It is only a candidate and may not be optimal.

commonMistakes.claim: A zero constraint gradient rules out extrema.
commonMistakes.correction: It invalidates regularity, not optimality. Check singular points separately.

practice.problem: Find the maximum of $x+y$ on the unit circle.
practice.hint: Use parallel gradients or a dot-product bound.
solution: $(1,1)\cdot(x,y)\le\sqrt2$.
Equality occurs at $(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)$.

practice.problem: Minimize $x^2+y^2$ on line $x+y=4$.
For constraint $x^2+y^2=0$, minimize $f=x$. Do ordinary multiplier equations find a candidate?
practice.hint: The feasible set is a single point.
solution: The origin is necessarily the optimum, but the constraint gradient is zero.
The objective gradient is nonzero, so the ordinary equations cannot hold.
practice.answer: No; inspect the singular point separately.

practice.problem: When may two-constraint multiplier necessary conditions be applied directly?
solution: All functions must be continuously differentiable and both constraint gradients independent there.
practice.answer: Under smoothness and independent constraint gradients.

learningCheck.question: What follows solving the multiplier equations?
choices: Compare values and check singularities, boundaries and existence
learningCheck.explanation: Multipliers give necessary conditions, not automatic optimality.

interactiveVisual.prediction: Must parallel gradients indicate a maximum?

teaching.explain: At an extremum, feasible tangents cannot increase the objective to first order; its gradient lies in the constraint-normal direction.

steps.title: Aligned candidate
steps.observation: Position aligns with $(2,1)$; the linear objective is maximal.

steps.title: Perpendicular direction
steps.observation: The objective is zero, neither maximum nor minimum here.

steps.title: Opposing candidate
steps.observation: Position opposes the objective gradient, giving the minimum.

lessons.title: Double integrals and Fubini's theorem
lessons.subtitle: Multiply height by small area and add
lessons.concept: A double integral accumulates density or signed height over a planar region into one number.
lessons.intuition: Single integrals sum strips; double integrals sum small patches, each contributing height times area.
objectives: Set up double integrals and averages
Exchange integration order under sufficient hypotheses

body.title: Volume or signed accumulation?
body.text: Nonnegative height gives volume beneath the surface. Negative values cancel positives. For geometric volume, specify upper and lower surfaces or integrate absolute height.

body.title: Why can integration be repeated?
body.text: A continuous function on a rectangle can be integrated in either coordinate order with equal results. More general cases need integrability hypotheses.

body.title: Computing an average
body.text: Divide the total integral by region area: the area-weighted average output, not merely center height.

formalDefinition.text: Multiply height by small area and add
formalDefinition.latex: \iint_R f\,dA=\lim\sum f(x_i^*,y_i^*)\Delta A_i=\int_a^b\int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\,dx,\quad f_{\rm avg}=\frac{\iint_R f\,dA}{\operatorname{area}(R)}
conditions: Here Fubini uses continuity on a closed rectangle. Riemann grid diameters tend to zero. Averages require finite positive area.

derivation.text: Fix the first coordinate and accumulate a strip.
Sum strips across the first direction.
Use constant density to check units.

workedExamples.title: An integral over a rectangle
workedExamples.problem: Integrate $x+y$ over $0\le x\le2,0\le y\le1$.

workedExamples.title: Average height
workedExamples.problem: Find the average of $f=x+y$ on that rectangle.
steps: Their quotient is $3/2$; averaging each coordinate separately agrees.

commonMistakes.claim: A double integral merely repeats the integral symbol.
commonMistakes.correction: Specify region, area element and integration order.

commonMistakes.claim: Every function permits arbitrary order exchange.
commonMistakes.correction: Continuity or other adequate integrability hypotheses matter, especially near singularities.

practice.problem: Find $\iint 2\,dA$ on the unit square.

practice.answer: The signed integral is zero, unlike absolute-height volume.

practice.problem: Can integration order be exchanged for a continuous function on a rectangle?
solution: Continuity on a closed rectangle gives integrability, and Fubini equates the orders.

learningCheck.question: Integrating constant one over a planar region gives what?
learningCheck.explanation: Each piece contributes its area.

lessons.title: General regions and changing integration order
lessons.subtitle: Draw the region before choosing inner limits
lessons.concept: Limits describe a region. Changing integration order requires reading its boundaries afresh.
lessons.intuition: Vertical and horizontal sweeps cover the same land, but their slice endpoints differ.

body.title: Which variables may inner bounds depend on?
body.text: Only the fixed outer variables. The inner variable cannot appear in its own bounds.

body.title: When must the region be split?
body.text: Split where a slice's boundary formula changes, or where holes produce disjoint intervals.

body.title: Why choose an order?
body.text: It may simplify a difficult inner integral. Preserve the region and density rather than mechanically swapping differentials.

formalDefinition.text: Draw the region before choosing inner limits
formalDefinition.latex: D=\{a\le x\le b,\ g_1(x)\le y\le g_2(x)\},\quad\iint_D f\,dA=\int_a^b\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)}f\,dy\,dx
conditions: A bounded closed region with piecewise smooth boundary and continuous integrand suffices here. Preserve the region, splitting as needed.

derivation.text: Write bounds as inequalities.
Solve for horizontal slice bounds.
The new limits describe the same triangle.

workedExamples.title: Simplifying a nonelementary inner integral
workedExamples.problem: Evaluate $\int_0^1\int_x^1 e^{y^2}dy\,dx$.
steps: Changing order gives region $0\le y\le1,0\le x\le y$.
Integrating the first coordinate first gives $\int_0^1ye^{y^2}dy=(e-1)/2$.

workedExamples.problem: Find the area of $0\le x\le1,x^2\le y\le x$.

commonMistakes.claim: Only swap the differential symbols.
commonMistakes.correction: Rebuild the limits too.

commonMistakes.claim: Outer bounds may depend on the inner variable.
commonMistakes.correction: Choose the independent outer range, then specify each inner slice.

practice.problem: Reverse the order in $\int_0^2\int_0^{2-x}f\,dy\,dx$.

solution: The region is a first-quadrant triangle.
Horizontal slices satisfy $0\le y\le2,0\le x\le2-y$.

solution: Fix $0\le y\le1$; then $\sqrt y\le x\le1$.

practice.problem: If a horizontal line meets two disjoint intervals, may one integral span from the far left to far right?
solution: It would include extra blank area.
Use two inner integrals or subdivide the region.

learningCheck.question: What comes first when changing order?
choices: Write inequalities or draw the region
learningCheck.explanation: Ensure the sweep covers exactly the original region.

interactiveVisual.prediction: Does changing scan direction alter area?

lessons.title: Double integrals in polar coordinates
lessons.subtitle: Sector area needs a radius factor
lessons.concept: Polar coordinates simplify circular boundaries, but actual patch area is radius times radial width times angular width.
lessons.intuition: For the same small angle, a more distant arc is longer, making outer grid cells larger.
objectives: Keep area factors and avoid repeated coverage

body.title: Why the radius factor?
body.text: A sector's radial side is the radial increment; its angular side is approximately radius times angle increment. Their product gives area scaling.

body.title: When is polar simpler?
body.text: Disks, annuli, sectors and radially symmetric functions. Translate first if the circle's center is elsewhere.

body.title: Can coverage repeat?
body.text: Angles repeat after full turns. Use nonnegative radius and a range covering the region once. Boundary overlaps of zero area are harmless.

formalDefinition.text: Sector area needs a radius factor
conditions: Radius is nonnegative; the smooth transformation is one-to-one except on negligible degenerate sets. The function is integrable; do not cover positive-area portions repeatedly.

derivation.text: Find the radial side length.
Find the angular side length.
Their perpendicular product gives the area element.

workedExamples.title: A disk integral
workedExamples.problem: Integrate $x^2+y^2$ over the radius-2 disk.
steps: The integrand becomes $r^2$; the area element supplies another $r$.

workedExamples.title: An annulus
workedExamples.problem: Find the area of $1\le x^2+y^2\le4$.

commonMistakes.claim: Replacing the coordinates finishes the substitution.
commonMistakes.correction: Transform the area element, including its radius.

commonMistakes.claim: Sweeping two turns is just an alternative notation.
commonMistakes.correction: It counts positive-area regions twice, doubling the integral.

practice.problem: Find the area of a radius-3 disk.
practice.hint: Integrate one, keeping the radius factor.
solution: $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^3r\,drd\theta=9\pi$.

practice.problem: Find $\iint(x^2+y^2)dA$ over the unit disk.
practice.hint: The area factor adds one radial power.
solution: $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1r^3drd\theta=\pi/2$.

practice.problem: Find the area of a radius-2 sector of angular width $\pi/3$.
practice.hint: Integrate radially, then multiply by angle width.
solution: $\frac{2^2}2\cdot\frac\pi3=\frac{2\pi}3$.

practice.problem: What happens if the unit disk is integrated over angles zero to $4\pi$?
solution: Every interior nonorigin point is covered twice, giving twice the actual value.

learningCheck.question: What is the polar area element?
learningCheck.explanation: Angular side length equals radius times angle width.

interactiveVisual.caption: Keep radial and angular increments fixed while moving a small polar sector outward.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Why is the same parameter cell larger at greater radius?

teaching.explain: Fixed angle widths sweep longer edges outward, producing the radius factor.

steps.title: Small radius
steps.observation: Its angular side is short at this radius.

steps.title: Unit radius
steps.observation: Angular side length equals the numerical angle increment times unit length.

steps.title: Larger radius
steps.observation: For equal angle width, the small patch area roughly doubles.

lessons.title: Density, centers of mass and inertia
lessons.subtitle: Define each patch's contribution first
lessons.concept: Density times area gives mass; multiplying by position gives first moment; multiplying by squared axis distance gives moment of inertia.
lessons.intuition: Equal-area patches may have different mass. Equal masses farther from an axis resist rotation more, so distance is squared.
objectives: Model mass and center of mass from density
Set up inertia about a specified axis

body.title: Is center of mass an ordinary coordinate average?
body.text: It is a mass-weighted average. Geometric symmetry identifies it directly only when the mass distribution has that symmetry.

body.title: Which axis defines inertia?
body.text: About the first axis use the second coordinate squared; about the second use the first squared; about the perpendicular origin axis use their sum.

body.title: Connection to probability
body.text: A nonnegative density integrating to one can be a probability density. Region probabilities and expectations use the same weighted integrals.

formalDefinition.text: Define each patch's contribution first
conditions: Density is nonnegative and integrable. Center of mass needs finite positive mass; inertia needs finite corresponding second moments. Use consistent length units.

derivation.text: Local density determines patch mass.
Divide weighted positions by total mass.
Squared distance to the vertical axis determines inertia.

workedExamples.title: A nonuniform lamina
workedExamples.problem: On the unit square with density $\sigma=2x$, find mass and center of mass.
steps: First-coordinate moment is $2/3$; second-coordinate moment is $1/2$. Divide by mass.

workedExamples.title: Disk inertia
workedExamples.problem: A radius-2 disk has uniform area density 3. Find inertia about its central perpendicular axis.
steps: Mass is $12\pi$; the inertia also equals $\frac12MR^2$.
workedExamples.answer: $24\pi$, with units mass times length squared.

commonMistakes.claim: Center of mass is always the geometric center.
commonMistakes.correction: Uneven density shifts it toward heavier material.

commonMistakes.claim: Every moment of inertia uses the same distance.
commonMistakes.correction: Use perpendicular distance to the specified rotation axis.

practice.problem: Find the mass of the unit square at uniform density 4.
solution: Area 1 gives mass 4.

practice.problem: Find inertia about the first axis of a unit square at density one.
practice.hint: Distance to that axis is absolute second coordinate.

practice.problem: If all density is multiplied by 5, does the center of mass change?
practice.hint: Cancel the common numerator and denominator factor.
solution: Mass and first moments all multiply by 5, leaving ratios unchanged.

practice.problem: What must a valid probability density satisfy?
solution: It is nonnegative and integrates to one over the full sample region.

learningCheck.question: Doubling all density changes the center of mass how?
learningCheck.explanation: Weighted totals and total mass scale equally.

interactiveVisual.caption: Unit-square density $\sigma=1+cx$; column heights show density and the bright point marks its mass-weighted center.
interactiveVisual.prediction: As density on the right increases, where does the center move?

teaching.explain: Center of mass averages positions by mass; inertia totals squared axis distances by mass.

steps.observation: The center of mass is at the square's center.

lessons.title: Triple integrals and spatial regions
lessons.subtitle: Count every small volume once
lessons.concept: Triple integrals accumulate spatial density. Integrating one gives volume.
lessons.intuition: Slice the solid into thin vertical columns, accumulate density in each, then sum the columns. Three integrals describe three coordinate sweeps.
objectives: Compute volume and total spatial density

body.title: Building limits
body.text: Draw the projection, then specify each point's allowed height interval. Split regions that cannot be described by one column, or change direction.

body.title: Mass versus volume
body.text: Integrating one gives volume; integrating volume density gives mass. Volume and area densities have different units.

body.title: Changing order
body.text: Continuous functions on bounded regular regions allow different orders, but each requires a fresh description of the same region. Other cases need integrability checks.

formalDefinition.text: Count every small volume once
conditions: Here the region is bounded, piecewise smooth and describable between graphs, with continuous integrand. More general regions may be subdivided.

derivation.text: Fix planar position and integrate a column.
Accumulate over its projection.
Use integrand one to check upper and lower surfaces.

workedExamples.title: Tetrahedron volume
workedExamples.problem: Find the first-octant volume $x+y+z\le2$.
steps: One choice of limits is $0\le x\le2,0\le y\le2-x,0\le z\le2-x-y$.
Integrate height, then the triangle, giving $\int_0^2(2-x)^2/2\,dx=4/3$.

workedExamples.title: Mass in a box
workedExamples.problem: Find the mass of $0\le x,y,z\le1$ with volume density $\rho=1+z$.
steps: The base has area 1, leaving mass $3/2$.

commonMistakes.claim: All triple-integral bounds must be constants.
commonMistakes.correction: Curved regions generally need bounds depending on outer variables.

commonMistakes.claim: Triple integrals compute surface area.
commonMistakes.correction: Volume elements accumulate spatial quantities; surface area needs a surface integral.

practice.problem: Find the volume of a side-2 cube.
solution: Multiply three side lengths to obtain 8.

practice.problem: Find $\iiint xyz\,dV$ over the unit cube.
solution: Each is $1/2$; their product is $1/8$.

practice.problem: For region $0\le z\le1-x-y$, what must its projection satisfy?
practice.hint: The upper height cannot be below the lower height.
solution: With nonnegative planar coordinates, require $x+y\le1$ too.

practice.problem: Does changing integration order change density units?
practice.hint: Does the region or physical quantity change?
solution: Only the sweep changes; density remains mass per volume.

learningCheck.question: Integrating one over a spatial region gives what?
learningCheck.explanation: Each contribution is a small volume.

interactiveVisual.caption: Move a horizontal slice through the first-octant tetrahedron $x+y+z\le1$.
interactiveVisual.prediction: If slice edge lengths halve, does area merely halve?
