steps.title: Top slice
steps.observation: The slice collapses to a point; the solid's integral remains valid.

lessons.title: Triple integrals in cylindrical coordinates
lessons.subtitle: A polar base plus height
lessons.concept: Cylindrical coordinates retain height and use polar coordinates horizontally. The volume element keeps one radial factor.
lessons.intuition: A small volume is a polar patch times height. Adding a dimension does not introduce another radial factor.

body.title: Suitable regions
body.text: Cylinders, cones, axial paraboloids and solids projecting to disks often simplify.

body.title: Writing height limits
body.text: Replace horizontal squared-distance expressions by radius and identify the upper surface. For a cone, height is proportional to radius.

body.title: What about the cone's vertex?
body.text: Angle degeneracy on the axis occupies zero volume and is usually harmless. A singular density still requires a convergence check.

formalDefinition.text: A polar base plus height
conditions: Use nonnegative radius and avoid repeated angular coverage. The integrand is integrable; outside degenerate sets the map is smooth and one-to-one.

derivation.text: The horizontal patch uses the polar area element.
Height introduces no further scaling.
Volume is area times height.

workedExamples.title: Volume beneath a paraboloid
workedExamples.problem: Find the volume of $x^2+y^2\le z\le4$.

workedExamples.title: Squared distance inside a cylinder
workedExamples.problem: Integrate $x^2+y^2$ over the radius-1, height-2 cylinder.
steps: The integrand is $r^2$; the volume element contributes $r$.

commonMistakes.claim: Cylindrical volume uses radius squared.
commonMistakes.correction: Only the horizontal polar area contributes radius; height has no extra scaling.

commonMistakes.claim: For a circular projection, change only bounds.
commonMistakes.correction: Transform the integrand and volume element too.

practice.problem: Find the volume of a radius-2, height-3 cylinder.
practice.hint: Check with base area times height.
solution: $V=4\pi\cdot3=12\pi$.

practice.problem: What radial limits describe the conical region between $z=r$ and $z=2$?
practice.hint: Require ordered lower and upper heights.
solution: $r\le2$ requires $0\le r\le2$.

practice.problem: Why is the angle nonunique on the cylindrical axis?
solution: Both horizontal components vanish for every angle.
practice.answer: This coordinate degeneracy is usually harmless to volume integration.

practice.problem: Does $\iiint r\,dr\,d\theta\,dz$ represent density one or density equal to radius?
solution: The final radius comes from the volume element; density is one.

learningCheck.question: Why is there one radius factor in cylindrical volume?
learningCheck.explanation: Angular increments correspond to arc lengths, requiring radius.

interactiveVisual.caption: A radius-1, height-2 cylinder with a horizontal polar grid. Slice area is always $\pi$.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Does height introduce another radial factor?

teaching.explain: The horizontal patch is polar; vertical extension just multiplies its area by height.

steps.title: Middle

steps.title: Top

lessons.title: Triple integrals in spherical coordinates
lessons.subtitle: Account for all three edge scales
lessons.concept: The spherical volume element contains distance squared and sine of inclination, arising from two different angular arcs.
lessons.intuition: Farther out, equal angle widths span more area. Near a pole, the azimuthal circle shrinks.

body.title: Why distance squared?
body.text: The radial edge is the distance increment. Each angular edge contributes one distance factor, giving its square.

body.title: Why a sine factor?
body.text: The azimuthal arc follows a horizontal circle of radius distance times sine of inclination. It shrinks to zero at a pole.

body.title: Checking bounds
body.text: Check radial distance, azimuth and inclination. A cone fixes inclination; planes or off-center spheres can give angle-dependent radial bounds.

formalDefinition.text: Account for all three edge scales
conditions: Inclination is measured from the positive vertical axis. Avoid repeated positive-volume coverage, require integrability and use radians.

derivation.text: The radial edge has no scaling.
The inclination edge follows a meridian.
The azimuthal edge follows a latitude circle.

workedExamples.title: Ball volume
workedExamples.problem: Find the volume of a radius-2 ball.

workedExamples.title: Squared distance inside a ball
workedExamples.problem: Integrate $x^2+y^2+z^2$ over the unit ball.
steps: Density is $\rho^2$; multiplying by volume element gives $\rho^4\sin\phi$.
The radial integral is $1/5$; the angular integral is $4\pi$.

commonMistakes.claim: Spherical coordinates only add one radius beyond cylindrical coordinates.
commonMistakes.correction: They also need sine of inclination to account for latitude-circle length.

commonMistakes.claim: Sweep inclination through a full turn.
commonMistakes.correction: This repeats coverage and reverses orientation. Standard nonnegative volume uses zero to $\pi$.

practice.problem: Find the unit upper-half-ball volume.
practice.hint: Inclination covers the northern half only.
solution: Take half of the full volume $4\pi/3$.

practice.problem: Which inclination describes cone $z=r$?
solution: $\cos\phi=\sin\phi$ in the upper half-space, hence $\phi=\pi/4$.

practice.problem: Why are azimuthal arcs short near a pole?
solution: It is $\rho\sin\phi$; the sine vanishes at the pole.
practice.answer: The circle about the axis becomes small.

practice.problem: When integrating squared distance, what is the radial power?
practice.hint: Density's square times volume's square factor.
solution: $\rho^2\cdot\rho^2=\rho^4$.

learningCheck.question: What is the approximate actual length of a spherical azimuthal edge?
learningCheck.explanation: It follows a latitude circle whose radius is horizontal projection length.

interactiveVisual.caption: Keep spherical radius and angular widths fixed while moving a small grid patch across latitudes.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Are equal angular patches equal in area at pole and equator?

teaching.explain: Two angular edges supply distance squared; the latitude edge supplies an extra sine.

steps.observation: Equal angle width gives a very short latitude edge.

steps.title: Midlatitude
steps.observation: The latitude radius increases.

steps.title: Equator
steps.observation: The azimuthal edge is longest; its sine factor is one.

lessons.title: General changes of variables and Jacobians
lessons.subtitle: Measure local area or volume scaling
lessons.concept: A Jacobian determinant gives a smooth coordinate map's local area or volume scaling. Integration uses its absolute value.
lessons.intuition: A parameter square becomes a small parallelogram. Two derivative vectors determine area; three determine volume.

body.title: The Jacobian matrix
body.text: Arrange each output coordinate's partial derivatives by input parameter. In two dimensions its determinant is signed area scaling from the two derivative vectors.

body.title: Why the absolute value?
body.text: A negative determinant means orientation reversal, not negative area or volume. Oriented surface integrals have separate direction rules.

body.title: When is direct substitution invalid?
body.text: A nonzero local determinant does not ensure no global overlap. Check one-to-one coverage; folded maps require branches and multiplicity accounting.

formalDefinition.text: Measure local area or volume scaling
conditions: Use a continuously differentiable map one-to-one in the interior with nonzero interior Jacobian. Boundary degeneracies are negligible; require integrability. In three dimensions use a third-order determinant.

derivation.text: Partial-derivative vectors map small parameter edges.
derivation.latex: d\mathbf r_u=\mathbf r_u du,\quad d\mathbf r_v=\mathbf r_v dv

derivation.text: Their parallelogram area is the absolute determinant.
Transform the function and region together.

workedExamples.title: Ellipse area
workedExamples.problem: Map the unit disk by $x=3u,y=2v$. Find image area.
steps: The original disk has area $\pi$; area scales sixfold.

workedExamples.title: A skew grid
workedExamples.problem: For $x=u+v,y=u-v$, find the image area of the parameter unit square.
steps: Use absolute factor 2 times parameter area one.
workedExamples.answer: 2; the sign indicates orientation reversal only.

workedExamples.title: Position-dependent scaling
workedExamples.problem: Let $x=u,y=(1+u)v$, $0\le u,v\le1$. Find image area and its integral $\iint_D y\,dA$.
steps: The inverse is $u=x,v=y/(1+x)$, so the image is $0\le x\le1,0\le y\le1+x$ and coverage is one-to-one.
$J=1+u>0$; area is $\int_0^1\int_0^1(1+u)\,dv\,du=3/2$. One point's factor is not a global constant.
Transform the integrand too: $y=(1+u)v$. Thus the integral is $\int_0^1\int_0^1(1+u)^2v\,dv\,du=\frac12\int_0^1(1+u)^2du=7/6$.

commonMistakes.claim: A negative determinant gives negative mass.
commonMistakes.correction: An unoriented area element uses the absolute determinant.

commonMistakes.claim: Nonzero determinant guarantees global one-to-one coverage.
commonMistakes.correction: It gives local information; global injectivity needs a separate check.

practice.problem: Find the area factor for $x=2u,y=5v$.
Find area scaling and orientation for $x=v,y=u$.
solution: The determinant is $-1$; absolute area factor is 1.
practice.answer: Area is unchanged and orientation reversed.

practice.problem: Is $x=u^2,y=v$ one-to-one on $-1\le u\le1$ for direct substitution?
solution: Positive and negative parameters give the same first coordinate, duplicating interior coverage.
Split branches; do not treat both as one coverage.

practice.problem: Find the volume factor for spatial scaling $x=2u,y=3v,z=4w$.
solution: The absolute determinant is $2\cdot3\cdot4=24$.

learningCheck.question: What if the Jacobian is negative in an area integral?
learningCheck.explanation: Unoriented area is nonnegative; the sign records orientation.

interactiveVisual.caption: The unit parameter square maps by $x=u,y=(1+cu)v$ to a trapezoid. Move $u$ and compare local factor $J=1+cu$ with total area $1+c/2$.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Why cannot one local factor multiply the whole parameter area when scaling varies?

teaching.explain: Derivatives map a small square to a parallelogram; its determinant measures the local expansion.

steps.observation: The map is the identity; local factor and total area are both $1$.

steps.title: Near the left
steps.observation: The left local factor is $1$, while total image area is $3/2$. Local and global factors differ.

steps.title: Move right
steps.observation: The right local factor is $2$, while total area stays $3/2$; integration accumulates the varying factors.

lessons.title: Vector fields and streamlines
lessons.subtitle: An arrow at every position
lessons.concept: A vector field assigns a vector to each point. A streamline's tangent follows the field at each point.
lessons.intuition: A wind map describes local velocities, not one trajectory. An initial position selects a particle's path.

body.title: What does arrow length mean?
body.text: It represents field magnitude. Display arrows may share a shortening factor to avoid overlap; state that factor. Normalized arrows do not preserve magnitudes.

body.title: Field versus trajectory
body.text: A field maps position to vector; a trajectory maps time to position. In an autonomous field, particle velocity equals the field at its current position.

body.title: Checking a streamline
body.text: Substitute the path into the field and compare with its derivative. Parallel vectors with a different factor may describe the same geometric streamline under reparameterization.

formalDefinition.text: An arrow at every position
formalDefinition.latex: \mathbf F:\mathbb R^n\supset D\to\mathbb R^n,\quad\mathbf r\prime(t)=\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))
conditions: Existence and uniqueness need continuity and local Lipschitz conditions. Continuous first partials suffice in the usual examples. Do not cross undefined field points.

derivation.text: Read the vector at the current position.
Express velocity as the path derivative.
The rotational field preserves squared radius.

workedExamples.problem: For $\mathbf F=(-y,x,0)$, is $\mathbf r(t)=(2\cos t,2\sin t,0)$ a streamline?
steps: Substitution into the field gives the same vector.

workedExamples.problem: For $\mathbf F=(x,y,z)$ with initial point $(1,0,1)$, find the trajectory.

commonMistakes.claim: Each arrow is a complete trajectory.
commonMistakes.correction: An arrow gives only local direction and magnitude.

commonMistakes.claim: Equal arrow directions imply equal magnitudes.
commonMistakes.correction: Parallel arrows can have different lengths; check formulas and scale.

solution: This gives $(2,-1,0)$.

practice.problem: Where does field $(-y,x,0)$ point at $(1,0,0)$?

practice.problem: For constant field $(1,0,0)$ and initial point $(0,2,3)$, find the trajectory.
solution: $\mathbf r=(t,2,3)$; the other coordinates stay fixed.

practice.problem: On the unit circle, how are field $(-y,x,0)$ and radial field $(x,y,0)$ related?
solution: $-xy+xy=0$; both are nonzero on the circle.

learningCheck.question: How are a vector field and one trajectory related?
choices: The field gives local velocity; an initial value selects a trajectory
The field defines only one point
learningCheck.explanation: A position rule and a time-dependent path are different objects.

steps.title: Pure rotation
steps.observation: Arrows are tangent to circles; radial contribution is zero.

steps.title: Rotation with outflow
steps.observation: Arrows now have tangential and radial components.

steps.observation: The outward component grows. The circle is a reference, no longer a streamline.

lessons.title: Scalar line integrals
lessons.subtitle: Accumulate along actual length
lessons.concept: A scalar line integral weights a wire's density by arc length. Reversing direction leaves it unchanged.
lessons.intuition: Divide a curve into short segments. Each contributes density times length; faster parameter motion gives a longer segment per time increment.

body.title: Why multiply by speed?
body.text: A parameter increment is not length. Arc length is speed times that increment. Omitting speed makes the result depend on parameterization.

body.title: Does reversal change the sign?
body.text: Not for scalar arc-length integration, since length is nonnegative. A signed integrand can still give a signed result.

body.title: A wire's center of mass
body.text: Integrate position times line density against arc length, then divide by mass. Repeated tracing accumulates repeatedly; it does not automatically describe one physical wire.

formalDefinition.text: Accumulate along actual length
conditions: The path is piecewise smooth and the function continuous along it. Avoid repeated tracing for a wire. Regular monotone reparameterization preserves the integral regardless of speed or direction.

derivation.text: Approximate arc length by short segments.
Multiply each length by density.
Sum and take a mesh limit.

workedExamples.title: A circular wire
workedExamples.problem: Find mass of a radius-2 circle at line density 3.
steps: Choose $\mathbf r=(2\cos t,2\sin t,0)$, with speed 2.

workedExamples.title: Density along a diagonal
workedExamples.problem: A segment runs from $(0,0,0)$ to $(1,1,0)$, with density $x+y$. Find mass.
steps: Use $(t,t,0)$ from zero to one; density is $2t$, speed $\sqrt2$.

commonMistakes.claim: The parameter differential is the arc-length element.
commonMistakes.correction: Multiply by speed unless the parameter already is arc length.

commonMistakes.claim: Reversing a path negates every line integral.
commonMistakes.correction: Scalar arc-length integrals stay unchanged; work integrals reverse sign.

practice.problem: Find mass of a length-4 segment at density 2.
Integrate one over a unit semicircle.
solution: A radius-1 semicircle has length $\pi$.

practice.problem: Reverse a unit semicircle. Does scalar integral $\int_C1\,ds$ change?
solution: Length does not change sign, so the value remains $\pi$.

practice.problem: What happens if a circular wire's mass integral traces it twice?
solution: Each segment contributes twice, giving twice the physical single-loop mass.
practice.answer: It doubles; use one traversal for the wire.

learningCheck.question: What happens to a scalar arc-length integral after reversal?
learningCheck.explanation: Length has no travel direction.

interactiveVisual.caption: Accumulate density one along a unit circle; the bright arc marks travel.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Does reversing the path make a wire's mass negative?

teaching.explain: Speed compensates for parameter rate; direction never makes length negative.

steps.title: A short arc
steps.observation: The integral of density one is the quarter-circle length.

steps.title: A semicircle
steps.observation: The integral increases with path length.

steps.title: A full turn
steps.observation: The full circumference is $2\pi$.

lessons.title: Work and vector line integrals
lessons.subtitle: Keep force along directed displacement
lessons.concept: A work integral dots force with each directed displacement. Reversing the path reverses its sign.
lessons.intuition: Pushing along motion gives positive work; opposing motion gives negative work; perpendicular force contributes none.

body.title: Connection to arc-length integrals
body.text: Directed displacement is unit tangent times arc length. Thus work integrates tangential force against length.

body.title: Must the path be straight?
body.text: Any piecewise smooth path can be parameterized. Evaluate the field along it and dot with velocity; endpoint forces alone do not suffice.

body.title: Does a closed path force zero work?
body.text: No. A continuously tangential force can do positive work around a circle. Conservative-field hypotheses give zero closed-loop work.

formalDefinition.text: Keep force along directed displacement
formalDefinition.latex: \int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_a^b\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r\prime(t)dt=\int_C\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf T\,ds
conditions: The field is continuous along an oriented piecewise smooth path. Reversal changes orientation. Unit tangents are defined on regular pieces.

derivation.text: A short-step work contribution is force dotted with displacement.
Write displacement using parameter velocity.
Reversal negates directed displacement.
derivation.latex: \int_{-C}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=-\int_C\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r

workedExamples.title: Pushing around a circle
workedExamples.problem: Find work of $\mathbf F=(-y,x,0)$ around a radius-2 counterclockwise circle.
steps: Choose $\mathbf r=(2\cos t,2\sin t,0)$; velocity equals the field.
The dot product is 4; integration gives $8\pi$.

workedExamples.title: Radial force on a circle
workedExamples.problem: Find work of $\mathbf F=(x,y,0)$ along the same circle.
steps: Radial field and tangential velocity are perpendicular.
Every local contribution is zero, hence the full loop's work is zero.

commonMistakes.claim: Integrating force magnitude gives work.
commonMistakes.correction: Take the signed component along displacement.

commonMistakes.claim: Every closed path has zero work.
commonMistakes.correction: A rotational field is a counterexample.

practice.problem: Find work of constant force $(2,0,0)$ along a straight path from the origin to $(3,1,0)$.
practice.hint: Dot constant force with total displacement.

practice.problem: For constant force $(2,0,0)$, find work along the straight return from $(3,1,0)$ to the origin.
solution: The return displacement is $(-3,-1,0)$, giving work $-6$.

practice.problem: Find work when force is always perpendicular to velocity.
solution: Every contribution is zero, so is the integral.

practice.problem: Find work around the unit circle clockwise in field $(-y,x,0)$.
solution: Counterclockwise work is $2\pi$.
Reversal gives $-2\pi$.

learningCheck.question: How does reversing the path change work?
learningCheck.explanation: Work accumulates directed displacement.

interactiveVisual.caption: Counterclockwise unit-circle motion in field $\mathbf F=(-y,x,0)$; tangential force does positive work.
interactiveVisual.prediction: How can work be nonzero when start and finish agree?

teaching.explain: Only force along each displacement contributes; perpendicular force does no local work.

steps.title: Counterclockwise motion
steps.observation: The rotational field pushes along the path, accumulating positive work.

steps.title: Half a revolution

steps.title: Complete loop
steps.observation: The path closes, but work is $2\pi$; it does not cancel.

lessons.title: Potentials, path independence and holes
lessons.subtitle: When are endpoints enough?
lessons.concept: For a field equal to the gradient of a single-valued function, work is final potential minus initial potential.
lessons.intuition: Each step's work is an increment of one function. Intermediate increments cancel, leaving endpoints.

body.title: Finding a potential
body.text: Integrate one field component, allowing the constant to depend on remaining variables. Match other components, then verify the full gradient.

body.title: Are equal cross partials enough?
body.text: On a simply connected open domain, a continuously differentiable curl-free field has a potential. Simply connected means every loop can contract to a point within the domain.

body.title: Why do holes matter?
body.text: Local zero curl can coexist with nonzero work around a hole. A global potential must be single-valued; a branched angle is insufficient.

formalDefinition.text: When are endpoints enough?
conditions: The potential is continuously differentiable on an open domain containing the piecewise smooth path. Inferring conservativeness from zero curl also requires a simply connected open domain and continuously differentiable field.

derivation.text: Apply the chain rule to potential along the path.
Use the single-variable fundamental theorem.
A loop has matching endpoints, giving zero difference.

workedExamples.title: Finding a potential
workedExamples.problem: For $\mathbf F=(2xy,x^2+2y,0)$, find work from the origin to $(1,2,0)$.
steps: The second gives $g\prime=2y$; thus $\varphi=x^2y+y^2$, with endpoint value 6.
workedExamples.answer: 6, for any path staying in the domain.

workedExamples.title: A hole counterexample
workedExamples.problem: On the plane without the origin, find work of $\mathbf F=(-y/r^2,x/r^2)$ around the unit circle.
steps: The field equals unit tangent on the circle, giving $2\pi$.
Local cross partials agree, but the hole prevents a single-valued global potential.

commonMistakes.claim: Matching cross partials make the domain irrelevant.
commonMistakes.correction: A hole can support nonzero loop integrals.

commonMistakes.claim: Integrating any one component automatically gives a potential.
commonMistakes.correction: Match every component and verify the gradient.

practice.problem: Find a potential for $(2x,2y,2z)$.
practice.hint: Look for the gradient of a sum of squares.

practice.problem: Find work of $(2x,2y,2z)$ from the origin to $(1,2,2)$.
solution: Final value $1+4+4=9$; initial value zero.

practice.problem: How can two potentials differ on a connected domain?
solution: Their difference stays constant along connecting paths.

practice.problem: On the punctured plane, does zero curl automatically imply zero loop work?
solution: A unit circle around the hole can give $2\pi$.
Local zero curl does not eliminate global circulation around holes.

learningCheck.question: When a global potential exists, what determines work?
learningCheck.explanation: The chain rule and fundamental theorem cancel intermediate increments.

interactiveVisual.caption: Field $\nabla(\frac12(x^2+y^2))=(x,y)$ does zero work around the unit circle; compare with the preceding rotational field.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Which field property supports zero closed-loop work?

teaching.explain: For a single-valued gradient field, work sums potential increments and leaves only endpoint difference.

steps.title: Path start
steps.observation: The radial gradient field has potential one here.

steps.title: Midway
steps.observation: Potential stays one on the unit circle; accumulated work is zero.

steps.title: Return to start
steps.observation: Zero loop work follows from a global potential, not closure alone.

lessons.title: Green's theorem and planar flux
lessons.subtitle: Replace boundary circulation by interior rotation
lessons.concept: Green's theorem converts positive boundary circulation to an integral of local rotation. A second form computes outward planar flux.
lessons.intuition: Split the region into cells. Shared edges have opposite directions and cancel, leaving the overall boundary.
objectives: Compute planar circulation and outward flux
Check hole boundaries and field smoothness

body.title: Choosing positive orientation
body.text: Keep the region on your left: counterclockwise outer boundaries and clockwise hole boundaries. Include every inner boundary.

body.title: Circulation versus flux
body.text: Circulation accumulates tangential components; flux accumulates outward normal components. They use different derivative combinations.

body.title: When is the theorem unavailable?
body.text: The field must be continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of the whole region. Excise undefined interior points and include the added boundaries.

formalDefinition.text: Replace boundary circulation by interior rotation
conditions: The bounded region has finitely many piecewise smooth simple closed boundary curves, oriented with the region left. The field is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of the closed region.

derivation.text: Apply the fundamental theorem to opposite rectangle edges.
Combine the other pair.
Subdivision cancels shared edges, leaving the boundary.

workedExamples.title: Elliptical circulation
workedExamples.problem: Find circulation of $\mathbf F=(-y,x)$ around the semiaxis-2 and semiaxis-1 ellipse counterclockwise.

workedExamples.title: Outward planar flux
workedExamples.problem: Find outward flux of $\mathbf F=(x,y)$ across the radius-3 circle.

commonMistakes.claim: Positive boundaries are always counterclockwise.
commonMistakes.correction: Outer boundaries are counterclockwise; hole boundaries clockwise.

commonMistakes.claim: Smoothness on the boundary alone suffices.
commonMistakes.correction: The hypotheses cover the interior and an open neighborhood too. Do not ignore singularities.

practice.problem: Evaluate $\oint x\,dy$ around the positively oriented unit square.
solution: Rotation density and area are both 1.

practice.problem: Evaluate $\oint_C x\,dy$ clockwise around the unit square.
solution: The reversed integral is $-1$.

practice.problem: For radial field $(x,y)$, find total outward flux from an annulus of radii 1 and 2.
practice.hint: Multiply area by divergence, including the inner boundary.
solution: Area $3\pi$ times divergence 2 gives $6\pi$.

practice.problem: If the field has a central singularity, can zero rotation density establish zero circulation?
practice.hint: Which set must satisfy the hypotheses?
solution: The interior hypothesis fails.
Excise a small region around the singularity and include its boundary contribution.

learningCheck.question: How is an inner boundary oriented?
learningCheck.explanation: The actual region stays on the left.

interactiveVisual.caption: Field $(-y,x)$ over a variable-radius disk. Circulation is constant rotation density two times area.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Does doubling radius double or quadruple circulation?

teaching.explain: Shared cell edges cancel, leaving the positively oriented outer boundary.

steps.title: Small circle
steps.observation: Rotation density stays two; circulation follows area.

steps.title: Unit circle
steps.observation: Circulation is $2\pi$.

steps.title: Large circle
steps.observation: Doubling radius quadruples both area and circulation.

lessons.title: Parametric surfaces and orientation
lessons.subtitle: Two parameter directions span a surface
lessons.concept: Two parameters generate a spatial surface. Their independent tangent vectors have a cross product giving the local normal.
lessons.intuition: A parameter mesh may tilt and stretch in space. Its tangent cross product gives both normal direction and area scaling.

body.title: Regularity
body.text: The two partial-derivative vectors must not be parallel: their cross product is nonzero. At parameter poles, change charts or handle negligible boundary degeneracies.

body.title: Why use multiple charts?
body.text: A sphere has no single ordinary rectangular chart that is regular everywhere and nonrepeating. Use pieces without positive-area overlap.

body.title: Orientation
body.text: Choose a normal side continuously across the surface. Swapping parameter order reverses it. A Möbius strip has no global continuous unit normal.

formalDefinition.text: Two parameter directions span a surface
formalDefinition.latex: \mathbf r(u,v)=\langle x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)\rangle,\quad\mathbf n=\frac{\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v}{\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|}
conditions: Charts are continuously differentiable with nonzero interior cross product, avoiding repeated positive-area coverage. Global flux needs an orientable surface with consistent piece orientations.

derivation.text: Fix one parameter to obtain a curve family.
The curve derivatives span the tangent plane.
Cross them for a normal; normalize for a unit normal.

workedExamples.title: Normal to a graph
workedExamples.problem: Find the upward normal of surface $\mathbf r(u,v)=(u,v,u^2+v^2)$.
steps: Their cross product is $(-2u,-2v,1)$, with positive vertical component.

workedExamples.title: Orienting a cylinder
workedExamples.problem: Orient the side of a radius-2 cylinder outward.
steps: Cross azimuth derivative with height derivative to get outward $(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,0)$.

commonMistakes.claim: The two parameter derivatives' cross product is a unit normal.
commonMistakes.correction: It generally also contains area scaling and is not normalized.

commonMistakes.claim: Swapping parameters only changes notation.
commonMistakes.correction: It reverses orientation and therefore flux sign.

practice.problem: Find a unit normal for plane parameterization $(u,v,0)$.
For $\mathbf r(u,v)=(u,0,v)$, find the normal in the stated order.
practice.hint: Cross the first and third basis directions.

practice.problem: Can a zero cross product be normalized?
solution: Its length is zero. Change parameters or analyze the degeneracy.

practice.problem: Do degenerate poles in a spherical chart mean the sphere is nonsmooth?
solution: Only the angular chart degenerates; other local charts describe the smooth sphere.

learningCheck.question: How does swapping parameter order change the normal?
learningCheck.explanation: The cross product is anticommutative.

interactiveVisual.caption: Parameter plane $\mathbf r(u,v)=(u,v,cu)$, showing both tangent vectors and upward unit normal.
interactiveVisual.prediction: When do projected and actual mesh areas agree?

teaching.explain: Two parameter directions span the local tangent plane; their cross product records normal and area scaling.

steps.title: Flat surface
steps.observation: The tangent plane is horizontal and the normal upward.

steps.title: Gentle tilt
steps.observation: The plane tilts; cross-product length exceeds one.

steps.title: Steeper tilt
steps.observation: The actual area per parameter area increases further.

lessons.title: Surface area and scalar surface integrals
lessons.subtitle: Measure actual parallelogram area
lessons.concept: A surface element is the length of the tangent cross product times parameter area. Scalar surface integrals add a weight.
lessons.intuition: A sloping roof exceeds its horizontal shadow. Cross-product length measures the local enlargement.
objectives: Compute surface areas and membrane masses

body.title: A height graph
body.text: Using horizontal coordinates as parameters gives the square root of one plus the squared partial derivatives as area factor.

body.title: Does orientation change area?
body.text: No. Cross-product length survives reversal, as does a scalar surface integral.

body.title: Which density?
body.text: A membrane uses density per actual surface area, not projected area. Divide by actual area for surface averages too.

formalDefinition.text: Measure actual parallelogram area
formalDefinition.latex: \iint_S f\,dS=\iint_U f(\mathbf r(u,v))\|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|dudv,\quad dS=\sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}\,dxdy
conditions: Use piecewise regular charts without repeated positive-area coverage, with continuous integrand. The graph formula needs a continuously differentiable height function.

derivation.text: Map small parameter edges to tangent vectors.
derivation.latex: d\mathbf r_1=\mathbf r_u du,\quad d\mathbf r_2=\mathbf r_v dv

derivation.text: Take their parallelogram area.
For a graph, cross-product length yields the radical factor.

workedExamples.title: A sloping roof
workedExamples.problem: Find the area of $z=2x+y$ above the unit square.
steps: The area factor is $\sqrt{1+4+1}=\sqrt6$; multiply by base area one.

workedExamples.title: Paraboloid area
workedExamples.problem: Find the area of $z=\frac12(x^2+y^2)$ over the unit disk.

commonMistakes.claim: Surface area equals projected area.
commonMistakes.correction: Include local tilt enlargement.

commonMistakes.claim: Downward orientation makes a scalar surface integral negative.
commonMistakes.correction: Its area element is unoriented; orientation does not negate it.

practice.problem: Find the area of $z=x$ over the unit square.
practice.hint: Use the square root of one plus squared slopes.
solution: Factor $\sqrt2$ times base area one.

practice.problem: A membrane has area 5 and uniform area density 3. Find mass.
Does reversing orientation change $\iint_S1\,dS$?
solution: Cross-product length is unchanged, so is area.

practice.problem: Does small horizontal projection imply small actual area?
solution: Tilt factors may be large; a vertical surface is not a graph over that horizontal plane.

learningCheck.question: Which part of a cross product gives the surface area element?
learningCheck.explanation: It measures actual area spanned by local edges.

interactiveVisual.caption: A unit parameter square on plane $z=cx$; compare projection and actual area.
interactiveVisual.prediction: As the roof steepens over a fixed base, how does area change?

teaching.explain: Actual patch area equals parameter area times tangent cross-product length, including tilt.

steps.title: Horizontal
steps.observation: Actual and parameter-square areas agree.

steps.title: Tilted
steps.observation: The area factor is $\sqrt2$.

steps.title: Steeper
steps.observation: Projection stays fixed while actual area factor becomes $\sqrt5$.

lessons.title: Flux and oriented area
lessons.subtitle: Accumulate only what crosses the surface
lessons.concept: Flux integrates the field's component along a chosen normal. Tangential flow does not cross the surface.
lessons.intuition: A field crossing a net head-on contributes most; flow along it contributes none. Reversing its front side reverses the sign.
objectives: Keep normal and area element consistent

body.title: Unit normal or cross product?
body.text: A unit normal needs the actual area element. The unnormalized parameter cross product already includes area scaling: do not multiply it again.

body.title: Outward on a closed surface
body.text: Normals point away from the enclosed material. On a cavity boundary they point into the cavity, not necessarily away from the origin.

body.title: Does zero flux imply no flow?
body.text: Tangential flow or cancellation of inward and outward flow can give zero net flux. Net flow differs from total crossing magnitude.

formalDefinition.text: Accumulate only what crosses the surface
formalDefinition.latex: \iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,dS=\iint_U\mathbf F(\mathbf r)\cdot(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)\,dudv
conditions: The surface is orientable and piecewise regular; the field is continuous on it. The parameter cross product must match the chosen normal; otherwise negate it.

derivation.text: Take the normal component.
Multiply by actual patch area.
Combine unit normal and area scaling.

workedExamples.title: Flux through a tilted plane
workedExamples.problem: Find upward flux of $\mathbf F=(0,0,2)$ across $z=x$ above the unit square.
steps: The dot product is constantly 2, so flux is 2. Tilt scaling is already included.

workedExamples.title: Radial field on a sphere
workedExamples.problem: Find outward flux of $\mathbf F=(x,y,z)$ through the radius-2 sphere.
steps: The unit normal is position divided by 2, so the normal field component is 2.

commonMistakes.claim: After using a parameter cross product, multiply by area scaling again.
commonMistakes.correction: The cross product already contains that factor.

commonMistakes.claim: Zero net flux means the field vanishes everywhere.
commonMistakes.correction: Tangential flow or balanced crossing can give zero net flux.

practice.problem: Find flux of constant field $(0,0,3)$ through an upward horizontal patch of area 2.
practice.hint: Multiply the normal component by area.

practice.problem: Find flux of constant field $(0,0,3)$ through a downward horizontal patch of area $2$.
solution: The value changes from 6 to $-6$.

practice.problem: Find flux of a horizontal field through a horizontal surface.
practice.hint: Dot it with the vertical normal.
solution: Every dot product is zero.

practice.problem: When using an unnormalized cross product for flux, must $\sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}$ be included separately?
practice.hint: Is the area factor already present?
solution: The cross product supplies direction and area scaling; another radical duplicates it.

learningCheck.question: How does reversing surface orientation change flux?
learningCheck.explanation: The chosen normal determines flux sign.

interactiveVisual.caption: Vertical field $(0,0,1)$ through upward patch $z=cx$; show unit normal and area factor together.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Must vertical flux increase as the tilted surface's area grows?

teaching.explain: Multiply the normal component by actual area; a parameter cross product already combines them.

steps.observation: The field crosses head-on; unit-parameter-patch flux is 1.

steps.title: Tilted patch
steps.observation: The normal component decreases while area grows; they compensate.

steps.title: Steeper patch
steps.observation: For fixed horizontal projection, flux stays 1 while actual area grows.

lessons.title: Divergence and curl
lessons.subtitle: Measure net outflow and local rotation separately
lessons.concept: Divergence measures net outflow per unit volume. Curl's normal component measures local circulation per unit area.
lessons.intuition: A tiny box measures excess outflow; a tiny paddle detects rotation. A field may have either, both or neither.
objectives: State local interpretations and smoothness hypotheses

body.title: Why is divergence a scalar?
body.text: Compare flow across three opposite face pairs, divide by volume, and sum the three directional expansion rates.

body.title: Why is curl a vector?
body.text: Rotation can occur about different axes. Its components describe circulation densities on the three oriented coordinate planes.

body.title: Hypotheses for the identities
body.text: For sufficient smoothness, gradients have zero curl and curls have zero divergence. Mixed-derivative cancellation requires continuity and cannot be extended across singularities.

formalDefinition.text: Measure net outflow and local rotation separately
conditions: Use continuously differentiable fields for the formulas and local interpretations. Identities need the relevant continuous second partials. These are classical derivatives, not distributional singularities.

derivation.text: Opposite-face flow differences use partial derivatives.
Small-loop circulation differences use cross partials.
Continuous second mixed partials cancel.

workedExamples.title: A radial field
workedExamples.problem: Find divergence and curl of $\mathbf F=(2x,2y,2z)$.
steps: The three pure partials are each 2, so divergence is 6.
Cross partials vanish, giving zero curl.

workedExamples.title: A rotational field
workedExamples.problem: Find divergence and curl of $\mathbf F=(-3y,3x,0)$.
steps: The vertical curl component is $3-(-3)=6$; the others vanish.

commonMistakes.claim: Curved field arrows imply nonzero curl.
commonMistakes.correction: Curl measures local circulation density, not streamline shape alone.

commonMistakes.claim: Zero divergence means no motion.
commonMistakes.correction: Strong rotation or balanced flow may have zero local net outflow.

practice.problem: Find divergence of $\mathbf F=(x^2,y,z)$.
practice.hint: Differentiate each component in its own coordinate.

practice.problem: Find curl of $\mathbf F=(y,0,0)$.
practice.hint: Take cross partials in the specified order.
solution: The vertical component is $Q_x-P_y=0-1=-1$.

practice.problem: Find the curl of a smooth gradient field.
solution: Each component subtracts equal mixed partials; continuous second derivatives give zero.

practice.problem: Can a singular radial field be assigned zero divergence at its singularity using its outside formula?
solution: An undefined field has no classical divergence there. An outside formula cannot fill the singularity.

learningCheck.question: Does zero divergence exclude local rotation?
learningCheck.explanation: A pure rotation has zero divergence but nonzero curl.

interactiveVisual.caption: A horizontal slice of spatial field $(-y+cx,x+cy,0)$; planar expansion gives divergence $2c$ and curl $(0,0,2)$.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Can one field expand outward while rotating?

teaching.explain: Divergence examines box outflow; curl examines loop circulation. They measure different things.

steps.title: Pure rotation
steps.observation: Vertical curl is two; divergence zero.

steps.title: Add expansion
steps.observation: A planar radial component adds positive divergence without changing curl.

steps.title: Stronger expansion
steps.observation: Net outflow increases while rotation density stays two.

lessons.title: Stokes' theorem
lessons.subtitle: Keep the boundary and choose an easier surface
lessons.concept: Stokes' theorem connects boundary circulation with curl flux through a surface.
lessons.intuition: Subdivide an open surface. Internal edges run in opposite directions and cancel, leaving the surface boundary.
objectives: Match right-hand orientation and replacement hypotheses

body.title: Matching boundary direction
body.text: Point your right thumb along the positive normal; curled fingers give positive boundary direction. Walking with your head along that normal keeps the surface on your left.

body.title: Replacing the surface
body.text: The replacement needs the same oriented boundary and a smooth field on the required neighborhoods. Do not cross singularities or invalid domains.

body.title: Does a closed surface have a boundary curve?
body.text: Its curve boundary is empty, so smooth curl fields have zero total flux through it. A visible silhouette is not a boundary curve.

formalDefinition.text: Keep the boundary and choose an easier surface
formalDefinition.latex: \oint_{\partial S}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot\mathbf n\,dS
conditions: The surface is piecewise smooth and orientable, with compatible piecewise smooth boundary orientation. The field is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of the surface. Include all boundary components.

derivation.text: Pull each small-patch line integral into the parameter plane.
Apply Green's theorem and simplify by the chain rule.
Cancel shared edges to obtain the full formula.
derivation.latex: \oint_{\partial S}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot\mathbf n\,dS

workedExamples.title: Replace a hemisphere by a disk
workedExamples.problem: For $\mathbf F=(-y,x,0)$, find circulation around the unit upper hemisphere boundary counterclockwise from above.
steps: The boundary is a horizontal unit circle; use an upward disk.

workedExamples.title: A tilted triangular plane
workedExamples.problem: For $\mathbf F=(0,x,0)$, take the first-octant triangle in plane $x+y+z=1$, with normal's vertical component positive.
steps: Flux equals its horizontal projected triangle area $1/2$.

commonMistakes.claim: Matching boundary shape is enough; ignore direction.
commonMistakes.correction: Reversing orientation negates both circulation and curl flux.

commonMistakes.claim: Every surface flux can use Stokes' theorem.
commonMistakes.correction: The theorem concerns curl flux, not arbitrary field flux.

practice.problem: Find closed-loop circulation of a constant field.
practice.hint: Its curl is zero and it is smooth everywhere.
solution: Stokes, or constant force dotted with total displacement, gives zero.

practice.problem: Find circulation of $(-y,x,0)$ around a horizontal radius-3 counterclockwise circle.
practice.hint: Multiply curl two by disk area.
solution: $2\cdot9\pi=18\pi$.

practice.problem: Can the compatible-orientation formula be used after reversing the normal alone?
solution: The right-hand rule fails. Reverse the boundary or negate one side.

practice.problem: Find total flux of a smooth field's curl through a closed sphere.
practice.hint: The sphere has no boundary curve.
solution: Stokes gives circulation over an empty boundary, hence zero.

learningCheck.question: What can replace a difficult surface in Stokes' theorem?
choices: A surface with the same oriented boundary and required field smoothness
learningCheck.explanation: Preserve the boundary and check smoothness; do not cross invalid regions.

interactiveVisual.caption: Field $(-y,x,0)$ on surface $z=c(1-x^2-y^2)$ above a unit disk, keeping boundary and upward orientation fixed.
interactiveVisual.prediction: Why is circulation unchanged when the interior bulges and area grows?

teaching.explain: Use a more convenient surface with the same oriented boundary, provided field smoothness holds.

steps.title: Flat disk
steps.observation: The surface is a disk; curl flux is $2\pi$.

steps.title: Raise the interior
steps.observation: The interior rises; boundary and curl flux stay unchanged.

steps.title: Higher surface
steps.observation: Actual area increases, but curl flux remains $2\pi$.

lessons.title: The divergence theorem and closed surfaces
lessons.subtitle: Replace outward boundary flux by interior net outflow
lessons.concept: The divergence theorem equates outward flux through a closed surface with the integral of divergence over its enclosed volume.
lessons.intuition: Split a solid into boxes. Shared faces have opposite outward normals and cancel, leaving the exterior shell.
objectives: Add missing pieces and handle cavities and singularities

body.title: Must the surface be closed?
body.text: The theorem needs the whole volume boundary. Add a missing cap, compute the closed flux, then subtract the cap's flux.

body.title: Cavity normals
body.text: Point outward from the actual material. On inner boundaries this means into the cavity, not always away from the origin.

body.title: Singularities
body.text: The field must be continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of the solid. A point-source field undefined at the origin cannot have enclosing flux declared zero from its outside divergence.

formalDefinition.text: Replace outward boundary flux by interior net outflow
conditions: The solid is bounded with piecewise smooth outward-oriented boundary. The field is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood including solid and boundary. Include cavity boundaries.

derivation.text: Apply the fundamental theorem to opposite box faces.
Add all three coordinate contributions.
Subdivision cancels oppositely oriented common faces.

workedExamples.title: Radial flux through a sphere
workedExamples.problem: Find outward flux of $\mathbf F=(x,y,z)$ through the radius-2 sphere.
steps: Multiply by volume $32\pi/3$, giving $32\pi$, matching direct calculation.

workedExamples.title: Adding a base
workedExamples.problem: Find outward flux of $\mathbf F=(0,0,z+1)$ through the unit upper hemisphere.
steps: Add its base disk. Divergence one gives total closed flux $2\pi/3$.
The base points down and the vertical field component is one, giving base flux $-\pi$.
Subtract base flux from closed flux to obtain $5\pi/3$.

commonMistakes.claim: An open-surface flux directly equals a volume divergence integral.
commonMistakes.correction: Close the surface first, then remove the added flux.

commonMistakes.claim: A one-point singularity can be ignored.
commonMistakes.correction: It may invalidate derivative hypotheses while retaining nonzero flux.

practice.problem: Find outward flux of $(2x,2y,2z)$ through the unit sphere.
practice.hint: Multiply divergence six by ball volume.
solution: $6\cdot4\pi/3=8\pi$.

practice.problem: Find net flux of a constant field through any regular closed surface.
solution: The field is smooth everywhere; its divergence integral is zero.

practice.problem: What happens to radial-field flux if a sphere is oriented inward?
solution: Magnitude is unchanged and sign reversed.

practice.problem: Where does a spherical shell's inner outward normal point?
solution: The inner surface borders the cavity, so its normal points toward the center.

learningCheck.question: To which surface does the divergence theorem apply directly?
choices: The full outward boundary of a volume
learningCheck.explanation: Open surfaces require adding and subtracting missing pieces.

interactiveVisual.caption: Radial field $\mathbf F=(x,y,z)$ through a variable-radius sphere. Arrows use common scale 0.22.
interactiveVisual.prediction: If radius doubles, why does flux grow by more than area's factor four?

teaching.explain: The shell's net outflow equals total net outflow of interior boxes; common-face contributions cancel.

steps.title: Small sphere
steps.observation: Radial flux scales as radius cubed.

steps.title: Unit sphere
steps.observation: Outward flux is $4\pi$.

steps.title: Large sphere
steps.observation: Doubling radius multiplies flux by eight; boundary field strength also increases.

lessons.title: Choosing an integral theorem
lessons.subtitle: Identify the integral, hypotheses and orientation
lessons.concept: Path work, curl flux and closed-surface flux are different objects. Identify dimension, direction and field before choosing a theorem.
lessons.intuition: Are you traveling along a line or crossing a surface? Does the surface have a boundary or close a volume? These questions eliminate unsuitable tools.
objectives: Match the theorem to the integral

body.title: When are endpoints simplest?
body.text: For a global potential field, use endpoint differences on open or closed paths. Otherwise inspect the path or another applicable theorem.

body.title: Green or Stokes?
body.text: Green concerns planar-region boundaries; Stokes concerns spatial-surface boundaries. Both connect circulation and local rotation, agreeing in the planar case.

body.title: What does divergence handle?
body.text: The full outward flux of a closed volume boundary. It integrates divergence, not curl. Close open surfaces with consistently oriented added pieces.

formalDefinition.text: Identify the integral, hypotheses and orientation
conditions: Each conversion requires its own domain, smoothness, geometry and orientation hypotheses. No formula removes these requirements.

derivation.text: The chain rule links potential to endpoints.
An oriented surface links curl to circulation.
derivation.latex: \int_{\partial S}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=\iint_S(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot\mathbf n\,dS

derivation.text: A complete boundary links divergence to volume.

workedExamples.title: One field, two integrals
workedExamples.problem: For $\mathbf F=(-y/2,x/2,z)$, find positive circulation around the unit horizontal circle and outward flux through the unit sphere.
steps: Divergence is 1, giving sphere flux equal to volume $4\pi/3$.

workedExamples.title: Choosing endpoints
workedExamples.problem: Find work of field $(2x,2y,2z)$ along any path from the origin to $(1,1,1)$.
steps: Subtract endpoint values to get 3; no surface is needed.

commonMistakes.claim: Use Stokes for every surface integral.
commonMistakes.correction: Only curl flux corresponds to boundary circulation; arbitrary flux does not.

commonMistakes.claim: Divergence and curl are interchangeable.
commonMistakes.correction: They describe net outflow and local rotation, with different types and geometric objects.

practice.problem: Which planar-region theorem suits boundary integral $Pdx+Qdy$?
practice.hint: The integral follows the boundary tangent.
solution: Use Green's circulation form if the field covers the region and orientation matches.

practice.problem: Which theorem suits outward flux through an entire sphere?
practice.hint: The object is a full closed surface.
solution: Use divergence if the field is continuously differentiable across the ball.

practice.problem: Must a conservative-field path be closed before computing work?
practice.hint: What does a potential already give?
solution: Endpoint potential difference gives work directly.

practice.problem: May a replacement surface cross a field singularity?
practice.hint: Do its hypotheses hold on the new surface?
solution: Check the required neighborhood's smoothness; do not cross invalid regions blindly.

learningCheck.question: Which theorem turns spatial closed-loop work into a surface integral?
learningCheck.explanation: Boundary circulation corresponds to curl flux.

interactiveVisual.caption: Field $(-y/2,x/2,z)$; surface $z=c(1-r^2)$ and its base enclose a solid. Compare boundary circulation with full outward flux.
interactiveVisual.prediction: If a fixed boundary keeps circulation unchanged, must closed-surface flux also stay unchanged?

teaching.explain: Identify line versus surface, boundary versus closure and available potentials before choosing a theorem.

steps.title: Flat
steps.observation: The unit-circle circulation is $\pi$; the enclosed solid degenerates to volume zero.

steps.title: Bulging
steps.observation: Circulation is unchanged; added-base volume and closed flux are $\pi/4$.

steps.title: Higher
steps.observation: Circulation stays $\pi$, while closed flux increases to $\pi/2$.

lessons.title: Conservation and local-to-global balance
lessons.subtitle: Net boundary outflow reduces the interior total
lessons.concept: The continuity equation connects local density change with divergence of flux. Integrating gives mass balance on a fixed region.
lessons.intuition: Mass loss from a fixed container equals net boundary outflow. Shrinking the container yields the same balance locally.
objectives: Connect the continuity equation to global conservation
Distinguish velocity flux from mass flux

body.title: Is the flux field velocity?
body.text: Mass flux is density times velocity. Velocity flux gives volume flow; varying density makes the distinction essential.

body.title: Connecting differentiation and integration
body.text: With sufficient smoothness, interchange time differentiation and volume integration on a fixed region. Then convert boundary outflow using divergence.

body.title: How do the volume's tools connect?
body.text: Gradient describes local scalar change; divergence local net outflow; volume integrals accumulate interiors; surface integrals accumulate boundaries. Solving the resulting PDE belongs to a later volume.

formalDefinition.text: Net boundary outflow reduces the interior total
formalDefinition.latex: \frac d{dt}\iiint_E\rho\,dV=-\iint_{\partial E}\rho\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n\,dS,\quad\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot(\rho\mathbf v)=0
conditions: The region is fixed with piecewise smooth boundary, without volume sources. Density and velocity have required continuous partials and permit differentiation under the integral. Moving boundaries or sources need extra terms.

derivation.text: Total mass derivative equals negative net boundary outflow.
Use divergence to convert to a volume integral.
Validity on arbitrary small fixed regions gives local balance.

workedExamples.title: Uniform expansion
workedExamples.problem: For velocity $\mathbf v=(x,y,z)$, spatially uniform density and initial density one, find a conserving density.
steps: The equation becomes $\rho\prime+3\rho=0$; initial data give $e^{-3t}$.

workedExamples.title: Mass change in a fixed ball
workedExamples.problem: For that model, find mass and outward mass flow in the unit ball.
steps: The boundary normal velocity is one, giving flux $4\pi e^{-3t}$.
workedExamples.answer: Mass derivative and outward flow have opposite signs and equal magnitudes.

commonMistakes.claim: Velocity itself is mass flux.
commonMistakes.correction: Multiply by density; their units differ.

commonMistakes.claim: Conservation means mass in every fixed region is constant.
commonMistakes.correction: Boundary exchange can change interior mass. Conservation is the full balance.

practice.problem: A source-free fixed region has outward mass flow 5. Find its mass derivative.
practice.hint: What sign does outflow have for interior mass?
solution: Mass decreases, giving derivative $-5$.

practice.problem: With constant velocity and density uniform in space and time, does continuity hold?
practice.hint: Inspect time change and divergence separately.
solution: Density's time derivative and constant-flux divergence are both zero.

practice.problem: For divergence-free velocity and spatially uniform density, can source-free density vary arbitrarily in time?
solution: Zero spatial gradient and zero velocity divergence force zero time derivative of density.
practice.answer: No; it must be constant in time.

practice.problem: An internal source creates mass at rate 2 while outward flow is 5. Find the mass derivative.
practice.hint: Include the source in the balance.
solution: Production minus outflow is $2-5=-3$.

learningCheck.question: Does decreasing mass in a fixed container violate conservation?
choices: Not necessarily; there may be net outflow
learningCheck.explanation: Conservation includes boundary exchange.

interactiveVisual.caption: Fixed unit ball, velocity $(x,y,z)$, density $e^{-3t}$. Compare interior mass derivative with outward mass flux.
interactiveVisual.prediction: As mass decreases, must the outward flow rate remain constant?

teaching.explain: Account for missing interior mass through boundary outflow or internal sources.

steps.title: Initial time
steps.observation: Density is one; mass and outward flow are positive.

steps.title: Later
steps.observation: Uniform density decays exponentially, reducing outward mass flow too.

steps.title: Final displayed time
steps.observation: Mass keeps falling; its derivative remains the negative of outward flow.
